inputs.description: Considering your total clinical experience with this particular population, how mentally ill is this patient at this time?
inputs.options_text: 1=Normal, not at all ill, 2=Borderline mentally ill, 3=Mildly ill, 4=Moderately ill, 5=Markedly ill, 6=Severely ill, 7=Among the most extremely ill

inputs.label: CGI-Improvement (CGI-I)
inputs.description: Compared to the patient's condition at admission/start of treatment, how much has the patient changed?
inputs.options_text: 1=Very much improved, 2=Much improved, 3=Minimally improved, 4=No change, 5=Minimally worse, 6=Much worse, 7=Very much worse

bands.meaning: 1=Normal, 2=Borderline, 3=Mild, 4=Moderate, 5=Marked, 6=Severe, 7=Extreme illness
Much or very much improved — treatment response
Minimally improved — partial response
No change to much worse — treatment non-response

citations.text: Guy W (ed). ECDEU Assessment Manual for Psychopharmacology — Revised. DHEW Pub. No. (ADM) 76-338. Rockville, MD: NIMH, 1976. Pages 218-222

entries.limitations: Single-item measure — may not capture all aspects of illness. Clinician-rated — subjective and depends on assessor experience. Lacks specificity — doesn't identify which symptoms are changing. Anchor definitions rely on clinician's 'total clinical experience' with the population — varies by clinician. CGI-I requires comparison to baseline — different from absolute severity. No patient perspective incorporated. Inter-rater reliability moderate (ICC 0.65–0.80). Doesn't differentiate between domains (e.g., mood vs. anxiety vs. psychosis). Sensitive to expectation bias (clinician may rate improvement based on knowledge of treatment assignment).

entries.name: VBAC Success Prediction (Grobman Calculator)
entries.purpose: Clinical prediction tool estimating the probability of successful vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC). Helps counsel patients and guide shared decision-making about trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) vs. elective repeat cesarean.
entries.formula_human:
Logistic regression model:
log(p/(1-p)) = β₀ + β₁(Age) + β₂(BMI) + β₃(Race) + β₄(Prior vaginal delivery) + β₅(Indication) + β₆(Preterm)
p = estimated probability of VBAC success

Calculated using web-based calculator (perinatology.com/calculators or MFMU network)

inputs.label: Race/Ethnicity
inputs.options_text: African American, Hispanic, White, Asian, Other

inputs.label: Indication for prior cesarean
inputs.description: Reason for index cesarean (arrest of dilation, arrest of descent, non-reassuring fetal status, other)
inputs.options_text: Arrest disorders, Non-reassuring fetal status, Other

bands.meaning: High probability of VBAC success — TOLAC reasonable option
Moderate probability — shared decision-making, consider individual factors
Low probability — elective repeat cesarean may be preferred, but not absolute contraindication to TOLAC
No absolute threshold for offering/withholding TOLAC — estimated probability should inform shared decision-making

citations.text: Grobman WA, Lai Y, Landon MB, et al. Development of a nomogram for prediction of vaginal birth after cesarean delivery. Obstet Gynecol. 2007;109(4):806-812. PMID: 17400840

entries.limitations: Race/ethnicity inclusion is ethically debated — may perpetuate disparities (race is not a biological determinant but reflects structural factors). Doesn't include factors like cervical status at admission, estimated fetal weight, indication for repeat cesarean, or interdelivery interval. Accuracy moderate (AUC ~0.75) — not highly discriminatory. External validation shows overestimation in some populations. Should inform but not replace clinical judgment and patient preferences. Doesn't account for uterine rupture risk (separate risk factor).
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — published academic tool

entries.name: Aldrete Score for Post-Anesthesia Recovery
entries.purpose: Standardized scoring system for assessing readiness of patients for discharge from the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU). Based on reversal of anesthetic effects.
entries.formula_human:
Aldrete Score = Activity (0–2) + Respiration (0–2) + Circulation (0–2) + Consciousness (0–2) + SpO₂ (0–2)
Maximum = 10

inputs.label: Activity
inputs.description: Ability to move extremities voluntarily or on command

inputs.label: Circulation
inputs.description: Blood pressure relative to pre-anesthetic baseline
inputs.options_text: 0=±50% of baseline, 1=±20-49% of baseline, 2=±20% of baseline

inputs.label: O₂ saturation (SpO₂)
inputs.description: Oxygen saturation on room air or supplemental O₂
inputs.options_text: 0=<90% even with supplemental O₂, 1=90-92% with supplemental O₂, 2=≥92% on room air or baseline on supplemental O₂

bands.meaning: Ready for PACU discharge (meets criteria for transfer to ward or step-down)
Not ready for discharge — continued PACU monitoring
Some facilities use modified versions adding pain control, PONV assessment

citations.text: Aldrete JA, Kroulik D. A postanesthetic recovery score. Anesth Analg. 1970;49(6):924-934. PMID: 5534693

entries.limitations: Binary/ordinal — doesn't capture fine gradations of recovery. Modified versions exist with variable items (pain, nausea, urinary output, temperature). SpO₂ criterion may not apply equally to patients with baseline hypoxemia. Activity criterion affected by regional anesthesia, neuromuscular blockade reversal. Doesn't predict readmission or late complications. Score ≥9 doesn't guarantee stability — clinical judgment essential. Doesn't capture surgical site-specific factors (drain output, airway compromise risk). May be insufficient for enhanced recovery pathways with early mobilization.

entries.name: Apfel Score for Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
entries.acronym: Apfel Score / Simplified Risk Score for PONV
entries.purpose: Simplified risk assessment for predicting postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in adult patients. Guides antiemetic prophylaxis strategy. Replaces more complex models.
entries.formula_human:
Apfel Score = Number of risk factors present (0–4)
Risk factors: female, non-smoker, history of PONV/motion sickness, postoperative opioids

inputs.label: Non-smoker
inputs.description: Patient is a non-smoker (or has not smoked in past 2 weeks)

inputs.label: History of motion sickness or PONV
inputs.description: Previous history of PONV or motion sickness

bands.meaning: ~10% risk of PONV. Low risk — no prophylaxis typically needed.
~20% risk of PONV. Low-moderate risk — consider single antiemetic.
~40% risk of PONV. Moderate risk — multimodal prophylaxis recommended.
~60% risk of PONV. High risk — multimodal prophylaxis + consider TIVA (total IV anesthesia), regional techniques.
~80% risk of PONV. Very high risk — aggressive multimodal prophylaxis, avoid volatile agents and opioids if possible.

citations.text: Apfel CC, Läärä E, Koivuranta M, et al. A simplified risk score for predicting postoperative nausea and vomiting: conclusions from cross-validations between two centers. Anesthesiology. 1999;91(3):693-700. PMID: 10485781

entries.limitations: Predicts PONV but not severity — doesn't distinguish nausea from vomiting. Risk factors are simplified — doesn't capture type of surgery, duration of anesthesia, or anesthetic technique in detail. Applies to adults only (separate pediatric score: POVOC score). Threshold for prophylaxis debated — SAMBA guidelines suggest prophylaxis for moderate-high risk patients. Doesn't incorporate regional anesthesia, TIVA, or specific antiemetics used. Gender factor cannot be modified. Historical PONV/motion sickness may be unreliable (patient may not know). Each risk factor contributes equally — some may be more important than others.
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — published academic tool

entries.name: Physiological and Operative Severity Score for the enUmeration of Mortality and Morbidity
entries.purpose: Comprehensive risk prediction model for surgical morbidity and mortality incorporating both patient physiological parameters and operative severity. P-POSSUM is Portsmouth modification calibrated for mortality prediction.
entries.formula_human:
Physiological Score (PS) = sum of 12 physiological variables (each 1, 2, 4, or 8)
Operative Severity Score (OS) = sum of 6 operative variables (each 1, 2, 4, or 8)

POSSUM Morbidity: ln(R/(1-R)) = -5.91 + (0.16 × PS) + (0.19 × OS)
P-POSSUM Mortality: ln(R/(1-R)) = -9.065 + (0.1692 × PS) + (0.1550 × OS)
where R = predicted risk

inputs.label: Physiological Score (12 variables)
inputs.description: Age, cardiac signs, respiratory signs, ECG, systolic BP, pulse rate, Glasgow Coma Score, Hb, WBC, urea, sodium, potassium

inputs.label: Operative Severity Score (6 variables)
inputs.description: Operative severity, number of procedures, blood loss, peritoneal contamination, malignancy status, timing (elective/urgent/emergency)

bands.meaning: Calculated from regression equation — R value represents percentage mortality risk
Predicts overall complication rate including minor and major complications
Low predicted mortality — standard perioperative care
Elevated predicted mortality — enhanced monitoring, HDU/ICU planning, shared decision-making

citations.text: Copeland GP, Jones D, Walters M. POSSUM: a scoring system for surgical audit. Br J Surg. 1991;78(3):355-360. PMID: 2021854; Whiteley MS, et al. Br J Surg. 1996;83:391-394 (P-POSSUM)

entries.limitations: Requires 18 variables — complex data collection. Operative variables only available postoperatively (limits preoperative use). POSSUM overpredicts mortality in low-risk patients (P-POSSUM corrects this). Doesn't predict specific complications (only overall morbidity). Validated primarily in general/vascular surgery — accuracy varies by specialty. Physiological variables may change rapidly (e.g., pre-op resuscitation). Emergency surgery has highest weight but lowest accuracy. Doesn't capture surgical skill, hospital volume, or process quality.
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — published academic tool

entries.name: Dermatology Life Quality Index
entries.purpose: Patient-reported 10-item quality of life measure for skin disease. Captures impact on symptoms, daily activities, work/school, relationships, and treatment burden. Used across all dermatological conditions.
entries.formula_human:
DLQI = Sum of Q1–Q10 (each 0–3)
Maximum = 30
If items unanswered: (sum / (answered items × 3)) × 30
Higher = greater QoL impairment

inputs.label: 10 questions about the past week
inputs.description: Each scored 0–3: 0=Not at all, 1=A little, 2=A lot, 3=Very much

inputs.label: Q8: Relationships/partner
inputs.description: Impact on relationships with partner/close friends

bands.meaning: No effect on QoL
Small effect on QoL
Moderate effect on QoL
Very large effect on QoL
Extremely large effect on QoL
Minimum clinically important difference

citations.text: Finlay AY, Khan GK. Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) — a simple practical measure for routine clinical use. Clin Exp Dermatol. 1994;19(3):210-216. PMID: 8033378

entries.limitations: Patient-reported — subject to recall bias. 7-day recall period. Questions about sport, work, and sexual difficulties may not be applicable (N/A option exists but may affect interpretation). Doesn't capture sleep disturbance directly (question 1 partially covers). Cultural variation in reporting embarrassment and sexual difficulties. Single skin condition at a time (doesn't capture multiple dermatoses). May not capture severe disfigurement or disease in non-visible areas (different from visible areas). Ceiling effect in severe disease. Dermatology-specific — not directly comparable to general QoL measures.
entries.copyright: Cardiff University — free for clinical use, permission needed for commercial/research applications

entries.name: Rumack-Matthew Nomogram for Acetaminophen Toxicity
entries.purpose: Treatment nomogram used to determine which patients with acute acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose require N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment based on serum acetaminophen level plotted against time from ingestion.
entries.formula_human:
Treatment line (original): Connects 200 µg/mL at 4 hours to 50 µg/mL at 16 hours (semilogarithmic plot)

Treatment line (Matthew modification): Connects 150 µg/mL at 4 hours to 37.5 µg/mL at 16 hours (used in USA, most centers)

Above treatment line at time point → NAC indicated
Below treatment line → NAC not indicated (in acute single ingestion with reliable history)

Key conversion: 200 µg/mL = 1320 µmol/L; 150 µg/mL = 990 µmol/L

inputs.label: Serum acetaminophen level
inputs.description: Serum acetaminophen concentration drawn at least 4 hours post-ingestion

inputs.label: Time from ingestion
inputs.description: Exact time from acute single ingestion to blood draw

bands.meaning: NAC treatment indicated — initiate NAC protocol (21-hour IV protocol or 72-hour oral protocol). Risk of hepatotoxicity ~60% without treatment.
NAC not indicated (in acute single ingestion with known time). Risk of hepatotoxicity minimal. Discharge if clinically well.
Nomogram NOT applicable — treat with NAC empirically and check acetaminophen level, LFTs
Nomogram NOT applicable — treat based on clinical status (ALT, INR, acetaminophen level)
UK uses 100-line (treatment line starting at 100 µg/mL at 4 hours) — more conservative

citations.text: Rumack BH, Matthew H. Acetaminophen poisoning and toxicity. Pediatrics. 1975;55(6):871-876. PMID: 1134884; Rumack BH. Pediatrics. 1978;62(5 Pt 2 Suppl):898-903

entries.limitations: Only valid for acute single ingestion with known exact time — not applicable for staggered/chronic ingestion. Requires serum level drawn at least 4 hours post-ingestion (earlier levels may be falsely reassuring). Time of ingestion must be reliably known — unreliable history makes nomogram unusable. High-risk patients (chronic alcoholism, malnutrition, enzyme inducers, fasting) may be at risk below the treatment line — some guidelines recommend treating these populations at lower thresholds. Does not account for co-ingestants (particularly those that delay absorption). Late presentation (>24 hours) requires clinical assessment rather than nomogram. Different treatment lines used internationally (150-line in US vs. 100-line in UK/Australia) — don't interchange.

entries.name: Hunter Criteria for Serotonin Toxicity
entries.purpose: Clinical diagnostic criteria for serotonin toxicity (serotonin syndrome) with higher sensitivity and specificity than older Sternbach criteria. Developed to standardize diagnosis in clinical and regulatory settings.
entries.formula_human:
Serotonin toxicity diagnosed if serotonergic drug context AND any of:
1. Spontaneous clonus
2. Inducible clonus + (agitation or diaphoresis)
3. Ocular clonus + (agitation or diaphoresis)
4. Tremor + hyperreflexia
5. Hypertonia + temp >38°C + (ocular or inducible clonus)

No numerical score — clinical decision tree

inputs.label: Serotonergic drug exposure
inputs.description: In the context of a serotonergic agent (SSRI, SNRI, MAOI, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue, etc.)

inputs.label: Hypertonia AND (temperature >38°C) AND (ocular clonus OR inducible clonus)

bands.meaning: Serotonin toxicity diagnosed — discontinue serotonergic agents, supportive care (benzodiazepines for agitation/rigidity, cooling, cyproheptadine), monitor for rhabdomyolysis and DIC
Serotonin toxicity not diagnosed — consider alternative diagnoses (NMS, anticholinergic toxicity, malignant hyperthermia, sympathomimetic toxicity)

Mild: clonus, tremor, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis. Moderate: temperature 38–40°C, agitation, mydriasis, bowel sounds hyperactive. Severe: temperature >40°C, severe rigidity, DIC, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, death

citations.text: Dunkley EJ, Isbister GK, Sibbritt D, et al. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: simple and accurate diagnostic decision rules for serotonin toxicity. QJM. 2003;96(9):635-642. PMID: 12925718

entries.limitations: Requires clinical assessment of neuromuscular findings (clonus, hyperreflexia) — may be difficult in sedated or uncooperative patients. Serotonergic drug context required — may miss cases with unusual agents or combinations. Temperature >38°C threshold may be too conservative — mild serotonin toxicity often afebrile. Doesn't quantify severity — grading system (mild/moderate/severe) is separate. May be difficult to distinguish from NMS (different mechanism) in patients on antipsychotics AND serotonergic agents. Cyproheptadine (5-HT antagonist) effectiveness is based on case reports only — no RCTs. Doesn't guide specific treatment decisions beyond stopping serotonergic agents. Clonus assessment requires cooperative patient.
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — published academic tool

entries.name: Rule of Nines for Burns
entries.purpose: Rapid estimation of total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns in adults. Used in emergency settings to guide fluid resuscitation (Parkland formula), triage, and transfer decisions.
entries.formula_human:
Adult Rule of Nines:
Head & neck = 9%
Each upper extremity = 9%
Anterior trunk = 18%
Posterior trunk = 18%
Each lower extremity = 18%
Perineum/external genitalia = 1%
Total = 99% (100% with rounding)

TBSA = Σ (region % × fraction burned in that region)

Pediatric modification (14 years and younger): Head = 18%, Each leg = 14% (increasing with age toward adult proportions)

Quick check: Patient's palm (including fingers) ≈ 1% TBSA (useful for scattered/irregular burns)

inputs.label: Body region burned
inputs.description: Percentage of each body region affected by second- and third-degree burns only (superficial/partial-thickness and full-thickness). First-degree burns excluded.
inputs.options_text: Head: 9%, Each arm: 9%, Anterior trunk: 18%, Posterior trunk: 18%, Each leg: 18%, Perineum: 1%

bands.meaning: Minor burn — can be managed at experienced burn center if no other factors
Moderate burn — requires IV fluid resuscitation (Parkland formula: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA in first 24 hours, half in first 8 hours)
Major burn — requires aggressive fluid resuscitation, burn center transfer. Consider intubation for >40% TBSA.
Any full-thickness >5%, burns involving face/hands/feet/genitalia/joints, circumferential burns, inhalation injury, electrical burns, chemical burns — all require burn center referral

citations.text: Wallace AB. The exposure treatment of burns. Lancet. 1951;1(6653):501-504. PMID: 14812587

entries.limitations: Overestimates TBSA in obese patients. Overestimates in children <14 years (head/leg proportions differ) — use Lund-Browder chart instead. Only applies to 2nd and 3rd degree burns (exclude 1st degree). Rapid estimation is inherently inaccurate — ±5-10% error common. Doesn't capture depth of burn (superficial partial vs. deep partial vs. full thickness). Doesn't account for burn mechanism, patient age, or comorbidities. Lund-Browder chart is more accurate for children and obese adults. Palm method (1% per palm) useful for small scattered burns but inaccurate for large areas.
entries.copyright: public domain — taught in all burn/trauma training programs

entries.name: Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status
entries.purpose: Simplified clinician-assessed performance status measure used in oncology for treatment eligibility, prognosis, and clinical trial stratification. Simpler than KPS (6 levels vs. 11).
entries.formula_human:
Grade 0: Fully active, able to carry on all pre-disease performance without restriction
Grade 1: Restricted in physically strenuous activity but ambulatory and able to carry out work of a light or sedentary nature
Grade 2: Ambulatory and capable of all self-care but unable to carry out any work activities; up and about more than 50% of waking hours
Grade 3: Capable of only limited self-care; confined to bed or chair more than 50% of waking hours
Grade 4: Completely disabled; cannot carry out any self-care; totally confined to bed or chair
Grade 5: Dead

inputs.label: Performance status
inputs.description: Patient's level of functioning in terms of ability to care for themselves, daily activity, and physical ability

bands.meaning: Fully active — eligible for all treatments including clinical trials
Restricted strenuous activity — usually eligible for most treatments
Ambulatory, self-care, no work — may be eligible for some treatments depending on cancer type
Limited self-care — most oncologists avoid cytotoxic chemotherapy. Focus shifts to palliative approaches.
Completely disabled — palliative/comfort care
Generally associated with worse prognosis across most cancer types

citations.text: Zubrod CG, Schneiderman M, Frei E, et al. Appraisal of methods for the study of chemotherapy of cancer in man: comparative therapeutic trial of nitrogen mustard and triethylene thiophosphoramide. J Chronic Dis. 1960;11:7-33; Oken MM, et al. Am J Clin Oncol. 1982;5:649-655

entries.limitations: Clinician-assessed — subject to inter-rater variability. Simple but may miss nuances (ECOG 2 includes a wide range of function). Binary thresholds between grades may not capture gradual decline. Patient and clinician assessments frequently disagree. Doesn't capture cognitive impairment, symptom burden, or psychological status. Cancer-specific — may not generalize to non-oncology populations. Doesn't predict treatment toxicity directly. Preference for ECOG vs. KPS varies by institution and clinical trial.
entries.copyright: ECOG-ACRIN — free for clinical use, published in standard oncology guidelines

entries.name: Palliative Performance Scale
entries.purpose: Clinician-assessed functional status measure specifically designed for palliative care patients. Extends Karnofsky Performance Status by incorporating ambulation, activity level, self-care, intake, and consciousness level.
entries.formula_human:
PPS levels: 100%, 90%, 80%, 70%, 60%, 50%, 40%, 30%, 20%, 10%

100%: Normal activity, full ambulation, full self-care, normal intake, full consciousness
90%: Normal activity with effort, full ambulation, full self-care, normal intake, full consciousness
80%: Normal activity with effort, full ambulation, full self-care, normal or reduced intake, full consciousness
70%: Reduced activity, unable to do normal job/work, full ambulation, full self-care, normal or reduced intake, full consciousness
60%: Reduced activity, unable to do hobby/housework, occasional assistance needed, normal or reduced intake, full consciousness or confusion/drowsy
50%: Reduced activity, unable to do hobby/housework, considerable assistance needed, normal or reduced intake, full consciousness or confusion/drowsy
40%: Unable to do most activities, mainly sit/lie, mainly dependent for self-care, reduced or minimal intake, full consciousness or confusion/drowsy
30%: Unable to do most activities, mainly in bed, mainly dependent, minimal intake, full consciousness or confusion/drowsy
20%: Unable to do any activity, totally bedbound, totally dependent, mouth care only, full consciousness or confusion/drowsy
10%: Totally bedbound, totally dependent, mouth care only, full consciousness or confusion or comatose
0%: Dead

inputs.label: Ambulation
inputs.description: Full, reduced, mainly sit/lie, mainly in bed, totally bedbound

inputs.label: Activity and evidence of disease
inputs.description: Normal activity, some activity, no activity, extensive disease

inputs.label: Self-care
inputs.description: Full, occasional assistance, considerable assistance, mainly dependent, totally dependent

inputs.label: Intake
inputs.description: Normal, reduced, minimal, mouth care only

bands.meaning: Cares for self, disease evident but some normal activity possible. Median survival weeks to months (cancer) to months-years (non-cancer).
Requires assistance, disease dominant. Median survival days to weeks.
Mainly bedbound, dependent. Median survival days. Focus on comfort care.
Associated with <3-month median survival in cancer patients. Consider hospice referral.

citations.text: Anderson F, Downing GM, Hill J, et al. Palliative performance scale (PPS): a new tool. J Palliat Care. 1996;12(1):5-11. PMID: 8857239

entries.limitations: Clinician-assessed — subject to inter-rater variability. Different diseases have different survival trajectories for same PPS score (cancer vs. non-cancer). Doesn't capture specific symptoms (pain, dyspnea, nausea). Cultural variation in reporting intake and activity. Doesn't incorporate psychological, spiritual, or social domains of palliative care. Validated primarily in cancer populations — may not be as accurate for non-cancer conditions. Cut-off for hospice referral (PPS ≤50%) may be too late for some conditions. Scoring across the 5 domains is not purely additive — some domains override others.
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — Victoria Hospice Society

entries.name: Palliative Prognostic Index
entries.purpose: Simple prognostic index for palliative care patients using clinical variables alone (no laboratory tests). Predicts survival probability based on performance status, oral intake, edema, dyspnea at rest, and delirium.
entries.formula_human:
PPI = PPS score (0–4) + Oral intake (0–2.5) + Edema (0–1) + Dyspnea at rest (0–3.5) + Delirium (0–4)
Maximum = 15

inputs.label: Oral intake
inputs.options_text: Unable to eat=2.5, Reduced intake=1, Normal intake=0

bands.meaning: Survival probability >50% at 3 weeks. Better prognosis.
Survival ~50% at 3 weeks. Uncertain prognosis.
Survival probability <50% at 3 weeks. Poor prognosis — comfort-focused care, hospice referral.

citations.text: Morita T, Tsunoda J, Inoue S, Chihara S. The Palliative Prognostic Index: a scoring system for survival prediction of terminally ill cancer patients. Support Care Cancer. 1999;7(3):128-133. PMID: 10335930

entries.limitations: Originally validated in Japanese palliative care patients — cross-cultural generalizability uncertain. Clinical variables are subjective (edema, dyspnea severity). Doesn't incorporate laboratory values. Validated primarily in cancer populations. Delirium assessment may be difficult in end-stage illness. PPS used as input inherits its limitations. Doesn't capture specific cancer type, treatment history, or advance care planning status. May not perform well in non-cancer palliative conditions.
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — published academic tool

entries.name: Palliative Prognostic Score
entries.purpose: Prognostic tool for terminally ill cancer patients estimating probability of 30-day survival. Helps guide goals-of-care discussions and resource allocation in palliative care settings.
entries.formula_human:
PaP Score = Dyspnea (0–1) + Anorexia (0–1.5) + KPS (0–2.5) + CPS (0–8) + WBC (0–1) + Lymphocyte% (0–2.5)
Maximum = 17

inputs.label: Clinical prediction of survival (CPS)
inputs.options_text: >12 weeks=0, 11-12 weeks=2, 7-10 weeks=2.5, 5-6 weeks=4.5, 3-4 weeks=6, 1-2 weeks=8

bands.meaning: Group A: 30-day survival probability >70%. Better prognosis — consider ongoing disease-directed therapy if appropriate.
Group B: 30-day survival probability 30-70%. Uncertain prognosis — consider best supportive care with possible targeted interventions.
Group C: 30-day survival probability <30%. Poor prognosis — focus on comfort care, symptom management, end-of-life planning.

citations.text: Pirovano M, Maltoni M, Nanni O, et al. A new palliative prognostic score: a first step for the staging of terminally ill cancer patients. J Pain Symptom Manage. 1999;17(4):231-239. PMID: 10203875

entries.limitations: Validated primarily in cancer patients — not applicable to non-cancer palliative care. Clinician survival prediction (CPS) is a component but is itself inaccurate. Laboratory values (WBC, lymphocytes) may be affected by infection, medications, and cancer treatment. Subjective symptoms (dyspnea, anorexia) vary by reporting. Doesn't capture specific cancer type, treatment history, or molecular markers. Doesn't account for psychosocial or spiritual factors. Requires recent blood work — may not be available in all palliative settings. Performance status measured by KPS inherits all KPS limitations.
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — published academic tool

entries.name: Hurtado Criteria for Q Fever Endocarditis
entries.purpose: Diagnostic criteria specifically for Q fever endocarditis caused by Coxiella burnetii. Modified Duke criteria may miss Q fever endocarditis — these criteria incorporate serological testing.
entries.formula_human:
Diagnosis of Q fever endocarditis:
1 definite: IgG Phase I ≥1:800 + histological/immunohistochemical evidence of C. burnetii on valve
1 possible + 1 minor = diagnosis:
- IgG Phase I ≥1:800 (major) + echocardiogram positive (minor)
- OR IgG Phase I ≥1:800 + ≥1 minor clinical criterion

inputs.label: Serology (Phase I IgG)
inputs.description: Anti-Coxiella burnetii Phase I IgG antibody titer

inputs.label: Clinical features
inputs.description: Fever, new cardiac murmur, embolic phenomena, immunological phenomena (Roth spots, Osler nodes), vascular phenomena

bands.meaning: Pathological evidence or IgG Phase I ≥1:800 + positive echo OR IgG ≥1:800 + fever + valve involvement
IgG Phase I ≥1:800 but insufficient additional criteria
Criteria not met or alternative diagnosis established

citations.text: Hurtado A, Carrion-Nessi F, Buitrago D, et al. Proposed modification of the Duke criteria for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis with Coxiella burnetii. J Infect. 2017;74:485-491; Raoult D, et al. Am J Med. 1991;91:401-405

entries.limitations: Specific to Q fever — not applicable to other causes of endocarditis. Phase I IgG ≥1:800 may not be available in all laboratories. Chronic Q fever serology takes weeks to evolve — early infection may be missed. IgG titer of ≥1:800 may also be present in chronic Q fever without endocarditis. Requires specialized laboratory (serology, PCR). Clinical presentation can be subtle (fever may be absent). Prosthetic valve involvement may be difficult to detect on echo. Treatment requires prolonged antibiotics (doxycycline + hydroxychloroquine for ≥18 months).
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — published academic criteria

entries.name: Modified McGeer Criteria for Infection Surveillance in Long-Term Care
entries.purpose: Standardized surveillance definitions for infections in long-term care facilities (LTCF). Revised in 2012 (Stone criteria) to improve specificity and applicability. Used for infection surveillance, outbreak detection, and quality improvement.
entries.formula_human:
No numerical score — diagnostic criteria met if specific clinical features and laboratory findings are present:

URI: ≥2 of 4 symptoms (cough, sore throat, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea) lasting ≤7 days
LRI: ≥3 of 6 symptoms; OR ≥2 + CXR infiltrate
UTI: Complex criteria depending on catheter status; requires positive UA + bacteriuria (≥10⁵ CFU/mL in non-catheterized, ≥10² in catheterized). NOTE: Asymptomatic bacteriuria should NOT be treated.
Skin/SSTI: Purulence or ≥2 inflammatory signs
GI: ≥2 GI symptoms
Fever: Temperature >37.8°C (100°F) or >1.1°C above baseline

inputs.label: URI criteria
inputs.description: Upper respiratory infection: ≥2 of cough, sore throat, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea AND ≤7 days duration

inputs.label: LRI criteria
inputs.description: Lower respiratory infection: ≥3 of cough, new/increased sputum, fever, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, crackles/bronchial breath sounds; OR ≥2 with CXR showing new infiltrate

inputs.label: UTI criteria
inputs.description: Urinary tract infection: ≥1 of dysuria, urgency, frequency, suprapubic pain with positive UA; OR ≥2 of fever, new/increased urinary symptoms, costovertebral tenderness, change in mental status with positive UA + significant bacteriuria

inputs.label: Skin/soft tissue criteria
inputs.description: Skin infection: purulent drainage or ≥2 of redness, warmth, swelling, tenderness

inputs.label: GI illness criteria
inputs.description: Gastrointestinal: ≥2 of diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, abdominal pain

bands.meaning: Surveillance definition of infection satisfied — report for infection surveillance, consider treatment
Does not meet surveillance definition — clinical judgment still applies
Surveillance definitions ≠ clinical diagnosis. Clinicians may treat based on clinical judgment even when surveillance criteria are not met.

citations.text: McGeer A, Campbell B, Emori TG, et al. Definitions of infection for surveillance in long-term care facilities. Am J Infect Control. 1991;19(1):1-7. PMID: 1850575; Stone ND, et al. Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol. 2012;33:965-977 (revised)

entries.limitations: Designed for surveillance, not clinical diagnosis — may miss early or atypical infections. UTI criteria complicated by asymptomatic bacteriuria (extremely common in LTCF — up to 50% of women). Change in mental status as UTI symptom is controversial and poorly specific. Doesn't capture healthcare-associated or device-associated infections specific to LTCF. Culture data often unavailable in LTCF — criteria require clinical judgment. Staff training needed for reliable application. Different criteria for different infection types — no unified scoring system. May miss infections in patients with communication difficulties (dementia).
entries.copyright: free for clinical use — published academic tool

entries.name: Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System
entries.purpose: Standardized quality assurance tool for mammography, ultrasound, and MRI reporting. Developed by ACR to standardize breast imaging terminology, reporting, and management recommendations. Ensures consistent communication between radiologists and clinicians.
entries.formula_human:
BI-RADS Categories:
0: Incomplete — need additional imaging or prior mammograms for comparison
1: Negative — no significant abnormality
2: Benign — definitely benign finding (cyst, fibroadenoma, calcified fibroadenoma)
3: Probably benign — <2% malignancy risk (round circumscribed mass, clustered round calcifications)
4: Suspicious — 2-95% malignancy risk
  4A: Low suspicion (2-10%)
  4B: Moderate suspicion (10-50%)
  4C: High suspicion (50-95%)
5: Highly suggestive of malignancy — ≥95% malignancy risk
6: Known biopsy-proven malignancy — for monitoring during treatment

inputs.label: Imaging findings
inputs.description: Description of breast lesion: mass, calcifications, architectural distortion, asymmetry, associated features (skin retraction, nipple retraction, skin thickening, axillary lymphadenopathy)

inputs.label: Lesion descriptors
inputs.description: Shape (oval, round, irregular), margin (circumscribed, obscured, microlobulated, indistinct, spiculated), density (fat-containing, low, equal, high), orientation, echo pattern (US), enhancement pattern (MRI)

bands.meaning: Incomplete — recall for additional imaging (spot compression, ultrasound, MRI). Does not represent final assessment.
Negative — routine screening in 1 year (for average risk). No action needed.
Benign — routine screening. Document benign finding.
Probably benign — short-interval follow-up (6 months) then annual if stable for 2 years. Biopsy if changes.
Low suspicion — tissue diagnosis recommended. Consider fine needle aspiration or core biopsy.
Moderate suspicion — tissue diagnosis recommended.
High suspicion — tissue diagnosis recommended urgently.
Highly suggestive of malignancy — tissue diagnosis needed. Should prompt biopsy without delay.
Known malignancy — monitoring during neoadjuvant treatment or post-diagnosis.

citations.text: American College of Radiology. ACR BI-RADS Atlas, 5th Edition. Reston, VA: ACR, 2013; D'Orsi CJ, et al. ACR BI-RADS Atlas: Mammography. 4th ed. 2003

entries.limitations: Inter-reader variability exists — different radiologists may assign different categories to the same study (moderate agreement for BI-RADS 3-5). BI-RADS 0 (incomplete) may lead to unnecessary recalls. Category 3 management (short-interval follow-up) may cause patient anxiety. Dense breast tissue (Category C or D density) affects sensitivity of mammography. BI-RADS density reporting mandated in many states but breast density alone doesn't determine cancer risk for individual patients. Digital breast tomosynthesis (3D mammography) may reduce recalls and improve specificity. MRI BI-RADS criteria differ from mammographic BI-RADS (enhancement kinetics). Doesn't apply to male breast imaging directly.
entries.copyright: ACR — free for clinical use with proper attribution

entries.name: Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System
entries.category: liver lesion classification in at-risk patients
entries.purpose: Standardized classification of liver observations detected on CT or MRI in patients at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Provides a lexicon, diagnostic algorithm, and management guidance. Applicable only in the setting of cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B, or prior HCC.
entries.formula_human:
LI-RADS categorization algorithm (per observation):

LI-RADS 1: Definitely benign
LI-RADS 2: Probably benign
LI-RADS 3: Intermediate probability of malignancy (could be HCC or benign)
LI-RADS 4: Probably HCC
LI-RADS 5: Definitely HCC

DIAGNOSTIC ALGORITHM (for ≥10 mm observations with imaging performed with extracellular contrast:
≥10 mm AND APHE AND washout = LI-RADS 5
≥10 mm AND APHE AND capsule = LI-RADS 5
≥10 mm AND APHE AND ≥50% growth in ≤6 months = LI-RADS 5
≥10 mm AND APHE but NO washout, NO capsule, NO threshold growth = LI-RADS 4
≥10 mm AND NO APHE but threshold growth = LI-RADS 4
≥10 mm with no major features = LI-RADS 3
10–19 mm AND APHE AND no other major features = LI-RADS 4

LI-RADS M: Probably or definitely malignancy, not specific for HCC (e.g., cholangiocarcinoma features)
LI-RADS TIV: Tumor in vein (definite tumor thrombus)

Ancillary features may upgrade or downgrade by 1 category (but cannot upgrade to LR-5 or downgrade from LR-5)

LR-5 observations in appropriate clinical context are DIAGNOSTIC of HCC per LI-RADS (meets AASLD criteria).

inputs.label: Observation size
inputs.description: Maximal diameter of the enhancing portion of the observation

inputs.label: Size ≥10 mm
inputs.description: Threshold for definite HCC using major features

bands.meaning: Definitely benign. No further workup needed.
Probably benign. Continue surveillance.
Intermediate. Follow-up imaging in 3–6 months or biopsy.
Probably HCC. Consider multidisciplinary discussion, biopsy, or empiric treatment.
Definitely HCC. Meets diagnostic criteria — no biopsy needed. Proceed to staging and treatment.
Probably malignancy, not specific for HCC (e.g., ICC or combined HCC-ICC). Biopsy recommended.
Definite tumor in vein. Diagnostic of malignancy.

citations.text: Chernyak V, et al. LI-RADS Version 2018. Radiology. 2018;289(3):816-830. PMID: 30398431; American College of Radiology. LI-RADS v2018

entries.limitations: Only applicable in patients with LI-RADS qualifying conditions (cirrhosis, chronic HBV without cirrhosis, current/prior HCC without cirrhosis). Not applicable to pediatric liver masses. Not applicable in patients with fibrosis from non-HBV causes (e.g., autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis) unless they have cirrhosis. Inter-reader variability exists (especially for washout and capsule). Equivocal observations (LR-3) require follow-up — cannot be definitively diagnosed. LR-M category was introduced to capture non-HCC malignancies but may limit sensitivity for certain HCC variants. MRI with hepatobiliary agents may reclassify some LR-3 to LR-4/5, but not all institutions have access. CT vs. MRI performance differs (MRI superior for small lesions). Imaging technique variability affects categorization. Does not replace biopsy in uncertain cases. Imaging surveillance intervals (every 6 months) are recommended for LR-1/2. Not validated for cholangiocarcinoma surveillance in PSC.
entries.copyright: ACR — free for clinical use with attribution

entries.name: Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System
entries.purpose: Standardized classification system for reporting and managing findings on low-dose CT (LDCT) lung cancer screening. Developed by ACR to standardize follow-up recommendations for pulmonary nodules detected during screening.
entries.formula_human:
Lung-RADS Categories:

1 (Negative): No pulmonary nodules. OR clearly benign nodules (calcified, fat-containing). Next LDCT in 12 months.

2 (Benign appearance/behavior): Solid nodule <6 mm, new solid nodule <4 mm, part-solid nodule <6 mm total, GGN <30 mm stable. Next LDCT in 12 months.

3 (Probably benign): Solid nodule 6-7 mm (baseline or new), part-solid nodule 6+ mm with solid <6 mm, GGN ≥30 mm stable or new GGN <30 mm. Next LDCT in 6 months.

4A (Suspicious): Solid nodule 8-14 mm (baseline or growing), part-solid nodule with solid 6-7 mm, new or growing GGN. Next LDCT in 3 months, PET/CT, or tissue sampling.

4B (Very suspicious): Solid nodule ≥15 mm (baseline or growing), part-solid nodule with solid ≥8 mm, or new/changed category 3/4. Chest CT ± PET/CT, tissue sampling.

4X: Category 3 or 4 with additional suspicious features (spiculation, lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion). Upgrade to higher suspicion.

inputs.label: CT findings
inputs.description: Nodule characteristics: size, morphology (solid, part-solid, ground-glass), location, growth compared to prior studies

inputs.label: Nodule size
inputs.description: Diameter of largest nodule (longest diameter for solid, average diameter for ground-glass/part-solid)

inputs.label: Prior comparison
inputs.description: Comparison with baseline or prior screening CT

bands.meaning: Negative — continue annual LDCT screening
Benign — continue annual LDCT screening
Probably benign — 6-month follow-up LDCT
Suspicious — 3-month LDCT, PET/CT, or biopsy consideration
Very suspicious — consider PET/CT and tissue diagnosis
Suspicious with additional features — recommend tissue diagnosis

citations.text: McKee BJ, McKee AB, Flacke S, et al. Lung-RADS: the radiologist's role in lung cancer screening. J Am Coll Radiol. 2015;12(1):29-35; Pinsky PF, et al. Radiology. 2018;287:1039-1047

entries.limitations: Applied only to LDCT lung cancer screening — not applicable to diagnostic CT. Nodule size measurement variability (inter-observer ±2-3mm). Part-solid nodule measurement of solid component can be difficult. Interval growth assessment requires comparison with prior study. Does not apply to non-nodule findings (bronchiectasis, emphysema — use separate reporting). Screening population is limited (USPSTF criteria: age 50-80, ≥20 pack-year history, currently smoking or quit within 15 years). Ground-glass nodules management debated — Lung-RADS may not capture all nuances. Patient anxiety with positive screens — requires counseling. False-positive rate significant at baseline screening.
entries.copyright: ACR — free for clinical use with proper attribution

entries.name: Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System
entries.purpose: Standardized interpretation and reporting of multiparametric prostate MRI (mpMRI). Stratifies the likelihood of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa, defined as Gleason ≥3+4) on a per-lesion basis. Guides biopsy decisions.
entries.formula_human:
PI-RADS assessment per lesion:

Peripheral Zone (PZ): DWI score is dominant
PI-RADS = DWI score (1–5). T2 and DCE are secondary.
T2 score 3 + DWI 3 + DCE positive = PI-RADS 4

Transition Zone (TZ): T2 score is dominant
PI-RADS = T2 score (1–5). DWI is secondary.
T2 3 + DWI 4/5 → upgrade to PI-RADS 4.
T2 3 + DWI 3 + DCE positive → upgrade to PI-RADS 4.

Anterior fibromuscular stroma / Central zone: Use TZ rules.

inputs.label: T2-weighted imaging score
inputs.description: Assessment of signal intensity and architecture on T2WI, scored 1–5. Scoring differs by prostate zone (peripheral zone vs. transition zone)

inputs.label: DWI/ADC score
inputs.description: Assessment of diffusion restriction on high-b-value DWI and ADC map, scored 1–5

inputs.label: DCE (Dynamic Contrast Enhancement)
inputs.description: Presence or absence of focal early enhancement on DCE. Only affects transition zone lesions with T2 = 3 + DWI = 3 (DCE+ upgrades to PI-RADS 4)

bands.meaning: Very low (clinically significant cancer highly unlikely). No biopsy.
Low (clinically significant cancer unlikely). No biopsy; clinical follow-up.
Intermediate (equivocal). Consider biopsy based on clinical factors, patient preference, prior negative biopsy.
High (clinically significant cancer likely). Targeted biopsy recommended.
Very high (clinically significant cancer highly likely). Targeted biopsy recommended.

citations.text: Weinreb JC, Barentsz JO, Choyke PL, et al. PI-RADS Prostate Imaging — Reporting and Data System: 2015, Version 2. Eur Urol. 2016;69(1):16-40. PMID: 26427182; Turkbey B, et al. PI-RADS v2.1. Eur Urol. 2019;76(5):592-598

entries.limitations: Requires experienced radiologist (minimum 100 prostate MRIs recommended). Inter-reader variability exists (especially PI-RADS 3). Does not detect all clinically significant cancers (up to 15-20% missed). MR-invisible prostate cancers exist (poorly differentiated without typical mpMRI features). PI-RADS 3 category has variable cancer detection rates (5-35%) across institutions. Does not substitute for systematic biopsy — combination of targeted + systematic improves detection. mpMRI quality dependent on scanner quality, coils, and sequences. Post-biopsy hemorrhage can mimic or obscure cancer. Lesion size and location affect detection. Not validated for active surveillance reclassification (separate criteria). Cost and access to prostate MRI limit universal application. Transperineal vs. transrectal approach not specified.
entries.copyright: European Association of Urology / American College of Radiology — free for clinical use

entries.name: Fleischner Society Guidelines for Incidentally Detected Pulmonary Nodules
entries.purpose: Management guidelines for incidentally detected solid and subsolid pulmonary nodules on CT. Provides size-based, risk-stratified recommendations for follow-up imaging and further workup. Not applicable to lung cancer screening populations (use Lung-RADS for screening).
entries.formula_human:
Management by nodule type and size:

SOLID NODULES:
</think>�<6 mm, low risk: No follow-up
<6 mm, high risk: Optional follow-up CT at 12 months
6–8 mm, low risk: Follow-up CT at 6–12 months
6–8 mm, high risk: Follow-up CT at 6–12 months, then CT at 18–24 months
>8 mm (any risk): Follow-up CT at 3 months, PET/CT, or tissue sampling

SINGLE SUBSOLID NODULE (GGN or part-solid):
</think>�<6 mm: No follow-up
≥6 mm: Follow-up CT at 6–12 months, then every 2 years for 5 years

MULTIPLE SUBSOLID NODULES:
</think>�<6 mm: Follow-up CT at 3–6 months. If stable, consider follow-up CT at 2 and 4 years
≥6 mm: Follow-up CT at 3–6 months. Subsequent management based on most suspicious nodule

inputs.label: Nodule type
inputs.options_text: Solid, Part-solid (mixed GGN), Pure ground-glass nodule (GGN)

inputs.label: Nodule size
inputs.description: Maximal diameter of the nodule on lung window (solid component for part-solid)

inputs.label: Number of nodules
inputs.points_text: Multiple nodules: follow dominant nodule; if ≥6 nodules, consider infection/metastases

inputs.label: Patient risk factors
inputs.options_text: Low risk (young, no smoking, no cancer history) vs. High risk (older, heavy smoker, prior cancer)

inputs.label: Nodule location
inputs.description: Upper lobe predominance (upper lobe nodule has slightly higher malignancy risk)
inputs.points_text: Not explicitly used in algorithm but considered in clinical judgment

bands.meaning: Very low risk. No further imaging recommended.
Low risk but clinical judgment may justify single check.
Indeterminate. If stable, additional follow-up at 18–24 months for solid; 2 and 4 years for subsolid.

bands.range: Follow-up at 3 months or PET/CT or biopsy
bands.meaning: Suspicious. Most nodules will still be benign, but active workup indicated.

citations.text: MacMahon H, Naidich DP, Goo JM, et al. Guidelines for Management of Incidental Pulmonary Nodules Detected on CT Images: From the Fleischner Society 2017. Radiology. 2017;284(1):228-243. PMID: 28240562

entries.limitations: Not applicable to lung cancer screening populations (use Lung-RADS). Does not apply to patients with known primary cancer (separate recommendations for metastatic surveillance). Does not address CT technique recommendations (slice thickness, reconstruction kernel). Subsolid nodule management with repeated CT over years may cause significant patient anxiety and radiation exposure. 6 mm threshold for subsolid nodules is somewhat arbitrary. Growth assessment of GGNs is difficult (contrast, slice thickness, inspiration level). Does not incorporate PET/CT for subsolid nodules (low FDG avidity in most subsolid malignancies). Not validated in immunosuppressed patients (e.g., transplant recipients — separate considerations). Atelectasis and infection may mimic nodule. Multiple nodule management can be confusing — follow the most suspicious. Prior comparison with older CT is essential but not always available. Does not address specific populations (e.g., patients with pulmonary fibrosis — ILA/IPF). Solid nodule growth rate doubles ~180 days for adenocarcinoma — 24-month stability may not be sufficient for all histologies. Biopsy of very small nodules has procedural risk exceeding benefit.
entries.copyright: RSNA — free for clinical use with attribution

entries.name: Bosniak Classification of Renal Cystic Masses
entries.purpose: Classifies renal cystic lesions based on CT/MRI imaging features to estimate probability of malignancy and guide management (surgery vs. surveillance vs. no follow-up). Updated in 2019 to improve reproducibility.
entries.formula_human:
Bosniak v2019 categorization (CT/MRI):

I: Simple cyst. Hairline-thin wall, no septa, no calcifications, no enhancement. Water density/attenuation.

II: Minimally complex cyst. Few (1–3) thin septa with possible perceived (not measurable) enhancement. Thin, smooth calcifications. Homogeneous high-attenuation lesions </think>�<3cm (≥70 HU) without enhancement.

IIF (Follow-up): Multiple thin septa (≥4) with possible perceived enhancement. Minimally thickened smooth wall or septa (1–2mm). Thick, nodular calcification without enhancement. High-attenuation lesions ≥3cm.

III: Cystic masses with thickened (>2mm) irregular wall/septa OR ≥4 thickened septa with measurable enhancement. Irregular calcifications.

IV: Cystic masses with enhancing solid/nodular component independent of wall/septa. Clearly enhancing solid component with a cystic component.

inputs.label: Wall characteristics
inputs.description: Thickness and regularity of the cyst wall
inputs.options_text: Hairline-thin, smooth / Minimally thickened / Thickened, irregular / Nodular

inputs.label: Septa
inputs.description: Number and characteristics of internal septa
inputs.options_text: None / Few thin septa / Multiple thin septa / Thickened septa / Nodular septa

inputs.label: Calcifications
inputs.options_text: None / Few thin / Scattered / Dense / Thick/nodular

inputs.label: Enhancement
inputs.description: Measurable enhancement after contrast administration (≥10 HU increase on CT or definite enhancement on MRI)

inputs.label: Number of septa
inputs.points_text: Bosniak IIF: ≤4 thin septa; Bosniak III: ≥4 septa or thickened

inputs.label: MRI characteristics
inputs.description: Signal on T1, T2, post-contrast (MRI can detect enhancement not visible on CT)
inputs.options_text: Simple (T1 dark, T2 bright, no enhancement) / Complex (variable)
inputs.points_text: May upgrade if MRI demonstrates enhancement

bands.meaning: ~0% malignancy. Benign simple cyst. No follow-up needed.
~0% malignancy. Minimally complex. No follow-up needed.
~5% malignancy. Follow-up imaging (3–6 months initially, then annually for 5 years recommended by some).
~50% malignancy. Surgical resection or biopsy recommended for good surgical candidates. Surveillance for poor surgical candidates.
~90% malignancy. Surgical resection (partial nephrectomy preferred).

citations.text: Bosniak MA. The current radiological approach to renal cysts. Radiology. 1986;158(1):1-10. PMID: 3510023; Silverman SG, et al. Bosniak Classification of Cystic Renal Masses, Version 2019: An Update Proposal and Needs Assessment. Radiology. 2019;292(1):143-151. PMID: 31012813

entries.limitations: Inter-reader variability exists (especially distinguishing IIF from III, and II from IIF). Perceived vs. measurable enhancement can be difficult to distinguish. CT technique affects categorization (thin-slice, multiphasic, iodinated contrast all important). MRI may detect enhancement not visible on CT, potentially upgrading category. Bosniak IIF represents a significant challenge — optimal follow-up duration debated. Category III is heterogeneous — approximately half are benign. Bosniak v2019 has not been universally adopted; many institutions still use 1986 version. Bosniak IIF and III are most controversial categories. Does not apply to solid renal masses (use RENAL nephrometry score or PADUA). Not validated for pediatric renal cysts. Not validated in patients with known syndromic renal cell carcinoma (VHL, BHD). Bosniak IIF follow-up duration and optimal imaging modality debated. US or MRI not validated as primary modality for Bosniak classification (CT is standard). Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) may improve categorization but is not formally included.

entries.name: RENAL Nephrometry Scoring System
entries.purpose: Standardized anatomical scoring system for renal masses to characterize surgical complexity. Predicts likelihood of successful partial nephrectomy vs. need for radical nephrectomy. Facilitates communication among surgeons and comparison across studies.
entries.formula_human:
R.E.N.A.L. Score = R + E + N + L (sum of 4 components, range 4–12)
Suffix: A, P, or X (anterior/posterior)
Suffix: h (hilar — touching renal sinus, applied to L component)

Total = R + E + N + L = 4–12

Low complexity: 4–6
Moderate complexity: 7–9
High complexity: 10–12

inputs.label: R (Radius)
inputs.description: Maximal diameter of the renal mass
inputs.options_text: ≤4 cm (1 point), >4 cm and ≤7 cm (2 points), >7 cm (3 points)

inputs.label: E (Exophytic/endophytic)
inputs.description: Degree of endophytic growth (percentage of mass not exophytic)
inputs.options_text: ≥50% exophytic (1 point), 50% exophytic (2 points), ≥50% endophytic (3 points)

inputs.label: N (Nearness to collecting system or sinus)
inputs.description: Closest distance of mass to the collecting system or renal sinus
inputs.options_text: ≥7 mm (1 point), 4–7 mm (2 points), ≤4 mm (3 points)

inputs.label: A (Anterior/posterior)
inputs.description: Location relative to coronal plane of the kidney

inputs.label: L (Location relative to polar lines)
inputs.description: Location of mass relative to the polar lines of the kidney
inputs.options_text: Entirely above upper or below lower polar line (1 point), Crosses polar line (2 points), >50% across polar line or crosses axial midline (3 points), Entirely between polar lines (suffix 'h' for hilar, touching renal sinus)

bands.meaning: Favorable anatomy for partial nephrectomy. High likelihood of successful nephron-sparing surgery. Consider partial nephrectomy as standard approach.
Partial nephrectomy feasible but technically more challenging. Experienced surgeon recommended. Discuss risks/benefits of partial vs. radical nephrectomy.
Very challenging partial nephrectomy. Consider radical nephrectomy vs. partial nephrectomy by experienced surgeon. Higher risk of complications (urine leak, hemorrhage, warm ischemia time >25 min).

citations.text: Kutikov A, Uzzo RG. The R.E.N.A.L. nephrometry score: a comprehensive standardized system for quantitating renal tumor size, location and depth. J Urol. 2009;182(3):844-853. PMID: 19616235

entries.limitations: Does not incorporate patient factors (comorbidities, renal function, age, CKD stage). Does not account for tumor histology (oncocytoma vs. RCC — imaging cannot reliably distinguish). 3D anatomy not fully captured (score is 2D-based). Does not predict oncologic outcomes (positive margins, recurrence). Inter-observer variability exists (especially for E and N components). Hilar tumors (suffix h) may be more complex than score suggests. Does not incorporate RENAL component into final number. CT acquisition protocol affects measurement. Does not incorporate tumor growth kinetics or patient preference. Centrally located tumors may be underestimated. Emerging: PADUA score, C-index, DAP score as alternative systems.
entries.copyright: public domain — published academic scoring system

entries.name: Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System
entries.purpose: Standardized ultrasound-based risk stratification for thyroid nodules. Guides decision for fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy or ultrasound follow-up. Aims to reduce unnecessary biopsies of benign nodules while not missing clinically significant malignancies.
entries.formula_human: TI-RADS points = Composition + Echogenicity + Shape + Margin + Echogenic foci (sum, range 0–14)

inputs.label: Composition
inputs.options_text: Cystic or almost completely cystic (0 points), Spongiform (0), Mixed cystic and solid (1), Solid or almost completely solid (2)

inputs.label: Echogenicity
inputs.description: Nodule echogenicity compared to adjacent thyroid parenchyma
inputs.options_text: Anechoic (0), Hyperechoic or isoechoic (1), Hypoechoic (2), Very hypoechoic (3)

inputs.label: Shape
inputs.options_text: Wider than tall (0), Taller than wide (3)

inputs.label: Margin
inputs.options_text: Smooth or ill-defined (0), Lobulated or irregular (2), Extra-thyroidal extension (3)

inputs.label: Echogenic foci
inputs.description: Presence of echogenic foci within the nodule
inputs.options_text: None or large comet-tail artifacts (0), Macrocalcifications (1), Peripheral (rim) calcifications (2), Punctate echogenic foci (3)

bands.meaning: No FNA recommended. Routine ultrasound follow-up if needed.
No FNA recommended. May follow with ultrasound if nodule ≥2.5 cm.
FNA if nodule ≥2.5 cm. Follow-up ultrasound if ≥1.5 cm.
FNA if nodule ≥1.5 cm. Follow-up ultrasound if ≥1 cm.
FNA if nodule ≥1 cm. Follow-up ultrasound if ≥0.5 cm.

citations.text: Tessler FN, Middleton WD, Grant EG, et al. ACR Thyroid Imaging, Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS): White Paper of the ACR TI-RADS Committee. J Am Coll Radiol. 2017;14(5):587-595. PMID: 28372962

entries.limitations: Inter-observer variability in subjective US features (especially echogenicity and margin). Spongiform composition category shows high specificity but may miss some follicular carcinomas. Does not incorporate clinical risk factors (radiation exposure, family history, rapid growth). Cystic papillary carcinomas may appear benign (TR1/2). Follicular carcinomas may lack classic suspicious features. Does not replace clinical judgment for nodules with concerning history even with low TI-RADS. Applies to thyroid nodules only — not lymph nodes or extrathyroidal masses. Some institutions use modified systems (K-TIRADS, EU-TIRADS). Should be combined with Bethesda cytology for final management.
entries.copyright: ACR — free for clinical use with proper attribution

entries.name: Clinical, Etiologic, Anatomic, Pathophysiologic Classification
entries.purpose: Standardized classification system for chronic venous disorders. Provides comprehensive clinical, etiologic, anatomic, and pathophysiologic description. Used for clinical practice, research standardization, and treatment planning.
entries.formula_human:
CEAP = C + E + A + P

Example: C6 Ep As,d Pr
(Active venous ulcer, primary etiology, superficial and deep veins, reflux)

Basic CEAP: Uses only the most relevant descriptor for each component.
Full CEAP: Uses all applicable descriptors for each component.

inputs.label: Clinical (C)
inputs.description: Clinical severity based on visible signs
inputs.options_text: C0: No visible signs; C1: Telangiectasias or reticular veins; C2: Varicose veins; C3: Edema; C4: Skin changes (C4a: pigmentation/eczema, C4b: lipodermatosclerosis/atrophie blanche); C5: Healed venous ulcer; C6: Active venous ulcer

inputs.label: Etiologic (E)
inputs.options_text: Ec: Congenital; Ep: Primary; Es: Secondary (post-thrombotic); En: No venous cause identified

inputs.label: Anatomic (A)
inputs.options_text: As: Superficial; Ap: Perforator; Ad: Deep; An: No venous location identified

inputs.label: Pathophysiologic (P)
inputs.options_text: Pr: Reflux; Po: Obstruction; Pr,o: Reflux and obstruction; Pn: No venous pathophysiology identified

bands.meaning: No visible or palpable signs of venous disease. May have symptoms (heavy legs, pain).
Telangiectasias/reticular veins. Cosmetic concern. Compression optional.
Varicose veins. Consider compression stockings, endovenous ablation, or sclerotherapy if symptomatic.
Venous edema. Compression therapy indicated. Investigate deep and superficial venous system.
Skin changes (pigmentation, eczema). Aggressive compression, consider intervention.
Lipodermatosclerosis/atrophie blanche. Advanced disease. Compression + specialist referral.
Healed venous ulcer. Lifelong compression to prevent recurrence.
Active venous ulcer. Multimodal wound care + compression + venous intervention.

citations.text: Eklöf B, Rutherford RB, Bergan JJ, et al. Revision of the CEAP classification for chronic venous disorders: consensus statement. J Vasc Surg. 2004;40(6):1248-1252. PMID: 15622385; Lurie F, et al. J Vasc Surg Venous Lymphat Disord. 2020;8:152-160

entries.limitations: CEAP is descriptive — it does not directly guide treatment decisions. Requires detailed clinical assessment including duplex ultrasound for accurate classification. C2 (varicose veins) is highly prevalent and heterogeneous — wide range of severity. C classification is ordinal but not linear (difference between C1→C2 ≠ C5→C6). Does not incorporate patient-reported outcomes (use VCSS, VEINES-QOL). Anatomic classification requires imaging (duplex ultrasound). Does not predict response to treatment. Primary vs. secondary etiology distinction not always clear. Venous Clinical Severity Score (VCSS) is more suitable for tracking treatment outcomes. Not validated in pediatric venous disease. Doesn't address pelvic venous insufficiency (may cause C2-C3 without lower extremity disease).
entries.copyright: American Venous Forum — free for clinical and academic use

entries.name: Venous Clinical Severity Score
entries.purpose: Clinician-assessed severity scoring system for chronic venous disease. Designed to track changes over time and assess treatment response. Complements CEAP classification (which is static and descriptive) by providing a dynamic, quantifiable measure.
entries.formula_human:
VCSS = Sum of all 10 items (each 0–3)
Range: 0–30

inputs.label: Pain
inputs.options_text: 0 (none), 1 (occasional, not restricting activity), 2 (daily, limiting some activities), 3 (daily, limiting most activities, requiring chronic analgesics)

inputs.label: Varicose veins
inputs.description: Size and extent of varicose veins
inputs.options_text: 0 (none), 1 (few scattered), 2 (multiple, involving below-knee GSV), 3 (extensive, above and below knee)

inputs.label: Venous edema
inputs.options_text: 0 (none), 1 (foot/ankle only), 2 (below knee), 3 (above knee or involving entire leg)

inputs.label: Skin pigmentation
inputs.options_text: 0 (none), 1 (limited to perimalleolar area), 2 (diffuse, lower third of calf), 3 (extensive, above lower third of calf)

inputs.label: Inflammation
inputs.description: Eczema, cellulitis related to venous disease
inputs.options_text: 0 (none), 1 (limited to perimalleolar area), 2 (diffuse, lower third of calf), 3 (extensive, above lower third of calf)

inputs.label: Skin induration
inputs.options_text: 0 (none), 1 (limited to perimalleolar area), 2 (diffuse, lower third of calf), 3 (extensive, above lower third of calf)

inputs.label: Active ulcers
inputs.description: Number and duration of active ulcers
inputs.options_text: 0 (none), 1 (1 ulcer </think>�<1cm, present </think>�<3 months), 2 (1 ulcer >1cm or 2–3 ulcers, or present 3–12 months), 3 (>3 ulcers or present >12 months)

inputs.label: Compression therapy
inputs.options_text: 0 (not applicable), 1 (intermittent use), 2 (wears most days), 3 (full compliance with stockings/bandages

bands.meaning: Mild venous disease.
Moderate venous disease.
Severe venous disease.
Very severe venous disease.
Extreme venous disease.

citations.text: Rutherford RB, Padberg FT, Comerota AJ, et al. Venous severity scoring: an adjunct to venous outcome assessment. J Vasc Surg. 2000;31(6):1307-1312. PMID: 10842165; Vasquez MA, et al. J Vasc Surg. 2010;51:1326-1331 (revised VCSS)

entries.limitations: Clinician-assessed — subject to inter-observer variability. Designed to complement CEAP, not replace it. Requires clinical expertise for accurate scoring. Compression compliance score (item 10) conflates treatment with severity. Pain is subjective. Not validated as a standalone diagnostic tool. Sensitivity to change may be insufficient for small differences (floor/ceiling effects). Not validated for superficial venous disease alone (designed for deep and superficial). May overestimate severity in patients with concomitant arterial disease. Not validated for pediatric venous disease. Recommended to score at baseline and follow-up (minimum 3-month intervals). Different scoring versions exist (original 2000 vs. revised 2010) — specify which version used.
entries.copyright: American Venous Forum — free for clinical and academic use

entries.name: House-Brackmann Facial Nerve Grading System
entries.purpose: Standardized grading of facial nerve function, particularly in the context of Bell's palsy, acoustic neuroma surgery, temporal bone trauma, and other facial nerve injuries. Accepted as the standard by the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (AAO-HNS).
entries.formula_human:
House-Brackmann Grade:

Grade I: Normal facial function in all areas
Grade II: Mild dysfunction (slight weakness noticeable on close inspection; slight synkinesis; normal symmetry at rest; forehead — moderate to good function; eye — complete closure with minimal effort; mouth — slight asymmetry)
Grade III: Moderate dysfunction (obvious but not disfiguring difference between sides; noticeable synkinesis/contracture; normal symmetry at rest; forehead — slight to moderate movement; eye — complete closure with effort; mouth — slightly weak with maximum effort)
Grade IV: Moderately severe dysfunction (obvious disfiguring weakness; normal symmetry at rest; forehead — no motion; eye — incomplete closure; mouth — asymmetric with maximum effort)
Grade V: Severe dysfunction (barely perceptible motion; asymmetry at rest; forehead — no motion; eye — incomplete closure; mouth — slight movement)
Grade VI: Total paralysis (no movement)

inputs.label: Gross facial function
inputs.description: Overall assessment of facial movement at rest and with effort
inputs.options_text: Grade I (normal) through Grade VI (total paralysis)

inputs.label: Forehead movement
inputs.description: Ability to raise eyebrows, wrinkle forehead

inputs.label: Mouth symmetry
inputs.description: Symmetry of mouth at rest and with movement (smile, pucker)

bands.meaning: Normal. No intervention needed.
Mild dysfunction. Good prognosis. Monitor.
Moderate dysfunction. Consider corticosteroids (if Bell's palsy). Prognosis generally good.
Moderately severe dysfunction. Corticosteroids ± antivirals. Consider electromyography (EMG) to assess prognosis.
Severe dysfunction. Aggressive medical therapy. Consider surgical decompression in select cases.
Total paralysis. Surgical exploration/decompression may be indicated. EMG/ENoG essential.

citations.text: House JW, Brackmann DE. Facial nerve grading system. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 1985;93(2):146-147. PMID: 3921901

entries.limitations: Only 6 grades — relatively coarse scale. May miss subtle changes (especially between grades II and III). Inter-observer variability exists (especially for grades III–V). Does not capture synkinesis severity independently. Does not include specific functional domains (corneal exposure risk, speech/eating difficulty, social impact). Newer systems (Facial Nerve Grading Scale 2.0 — FNGS 2.0, Sydney, Sunnybrook) offer more granularity. Not validated for bilateral facial paralysis. Doesn't capture dynamic changes over time without serial measurements. Subjective assessment — depends on examiner experience. May not detect partial paresis in specific nerve branches. Does not incorporate patient-reported quality of life. Some patients with HB Grade III have significant functional impairment (incomplete eye closure) that is underweighted.
entries.copyright: public domain — published academic grading system

entries.name: Abbreviated Profile of Hearing Aid Benefit
entries.purpose: Patient-reported questionnaire measuring hearing aid benefit across four listening situations. Used to quantify benefit from hearing aid fitting in clinical practice and research. Assesses both unaided and aided difficulty.
entries.formula_human:
For each subscale:
Score = (Mean of 6 items - 1) / 6 × 100

Benefit = Unaided score - Aided score (for EC, RV, BN only — AV excluded from benefit calculation)

Global benefit = Mean of EC, RV, and BN benefit scores

MCID for benefit: ≥5 percentage points

inputs.label: 24 items across 4 subscales
inputs.description: Each item rated on a 7-point scale (1=always, 7=never) for unaided and aided conditions

inputs.label: Ease of communication (EC)
inputs.description: Communication in favorable listening conditions (6 items)

inputs.label: Aversiveness of sounds (AV)
inputs.description: Negative reactions to environmental sounds (6 items)

bands.meaning: Substantial hearing aid benefit. Successful fitting.
Moderate benefit. Clinically meaningful improvement.
Minimal benefit. May need adjustment of hearing aid programming or counseling.
Persistent difficulty even with hearing aid. Consider alternative technology or aural rehabilitation.
Sounds are too loud/uncomfortable. May need compression adjustment or loudness discomfort management.

citations.text: Cox RM, Alexander GC. The Abbreviated Profile of Hearing Aid Benefit. Ear Hear. 1995;16(2):176-186. PMID: 7789673

entries.limitations: Patient-reported — subjective. Does not measure speech intelligibility directly. AV subscale cannot be used for benefit calculation (different direction). Does not capture directional microphone benefit or noise reduction algorithms specifically. Self-report bias (social desirability, expectation). Not validated for cochlear implant outcomes. Does not capture all listening situations (e.g., music appreciation, telephone). Different versions exist (APHAB-1995 vs. updated). Not validated in all languages. May be affected by cognitive status of respondent. Does not account for unilateral vs. bilateral hearing aid benefit separately.
entries.copyright: public domain — freely available for clinical and research use

entries.name: AAO-HNS Hearing Classification for Acoustic Neuroma
entries.purpose: Standardized hearing classification system for reporting hearing outcomes in patients with vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma). Classifies hearing based on pure-tone average (PTA) and speech discrimination score (SDS).
entries.formula_human:
AAO-HNS Hearing Class:

Class A: PTA ≤30 dB AND SDS ≥70%
Class B: PTA >30 dB and ≤50 dB AND SDS ≥50%
Class C: PTA ≥50 dB AND SDS ≥50%
Class D: PTA any level AND SDS </think>�<50%
Class E: No measurable hearing (dead ear)

inputs.label: Pure-tone average (PTA)
inputs.description: Average of air conduction thresholds at 500, 1000, 2000, and 3000 Hz

inputs.label: Speech discrimination score (SDS)
inputs.description: Percentage of words correctly identified at suprathreshold levels

bands.meaning: Good hearing. Serviceable hearing preserved.
Useful hearing. Serviceable hearing preserved.
Non-serviceable hearing (can detect speech but poor discrimination). Hearing preservation not expected.
Non-serviceable hearing. Poor speech understanding.
Dead ear. No functional hearing.

citations.text: Committee on Hearing and Equilibrium. Committee on Hearing and Equilibrium guidelines for the evaluation of hearing preservation in acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 1995;113(3):179-180. PMID: 7675485

entries.limitations: Does not capture tinnitus, aural fullness, or vestibular symptoms. Uses 3000 Hz in PTA calculation (less commonly tested than 4000 Hz). Class A and B together represent 'serviceable' hearing — class C–E is 'non-serviceable.' Class C may have useful hearing for some patients (heterogeneous group). Does not incorporate patient-reported hearing handicap. No distinction between class D and E functionally (both non-serviceable). SDS testing methodology varies (word lists, presentation levels). Doesn't capture bimodal hearing or cochlear implant candidacy. Newer systems (Gardner-Robertson, Tokyo, AAO-HNS 2012 update) exist but AAO-HNS remains most widely used. Not validated for other causes of hearing loss.

entries.name: Rutherford Classification of Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia
entries.purpose: Standardized classification of chronic limb ischemia severity based on clinical symptoms and objective testing. Used alongside Fontaine classification for clinical trial design, treatment decision-making, and outcomes reporting.
entries.formula_human:
Rutherford Category assigned by clinical presentation:

Category 0: Asymptomatic (objective PAD confirmed by ABI, duplex, or imaging)
Category 1: Mild claudication
Category 2: Moderate claudication
Category 3: Severe claudication
Category 4: Ischemic rest pain (ABI ≤0.40, ankle pressure </think>�<50 mmHg, toe pressure </think>�<30 mmHg)
Category 5: Minor tissue loss (non-healing ulcer, focal gangrene with diffuse pedal ischemia; ankle pressure </think>�<60 mmHg, toe pressure </think>�<40 mmHg)
Category 6: Major tissue loss (extending above transmetatarsal level; functional foot no longer salvageable)

inputs.label: Clinical symptoms
inputs.description: Walking ability, rest pain, and tissue loss
inputs.options_text: Asymptomatic / Claudication / Ischemic rest pain / Minor tissue loss / Major tissue loss

inputs.label: ABI / objective testing
inputs.description: Ankle systolic pressure, toe pressure, TcPO₂

bands.meaning: Asymptomatic PAD. Medical management (antiplatelet, statin, risk factor modification, exercise program).
Intermittent claudication. Supervised exercise therapy first line. Revascularization if lifestyle-limiting and refractory.
Critical limb ischemia (CLI). Rest pain. Urgent revascularization indicated.
CLI with minor tissue loss. Urgent revascularization. Wound care.
CLI with major tissue loss. Major amputation may be inevitable. Revascularization attempt if any foot salvage possible.

citations.text: Rutherford RB, Baker JD, Ernst C, et al. Recommended standards for reports dealing with lower extremity ischemia: revised version. J Vasc Surg. 1997;26(3):517-538. PMID: 9308598

entries.limitations: Subjective categories for claudication severity (mild, moderate, severe) — not precisely defined. Category assignment may vary between clinicians. Does not incorporate anatomic level of disease (inflow vs. outflow). Fontaine classification is simpler but less granular. Tissue loss assessment requires clinical examination — subjective. Categories 5 and 6 overlap in clinical practice. Not validated for acute limb ischemia (different classification). Does not incorporate wound healing potential (WIfI classification now preferred for predicting outcomes). Revascularization decision depends on anatomy (TASC II) + comorbidities — Rutherford alone insufficient. Doesn't capture patient functional status or frailty. Rutherford 4 (rest pain) vs. 5 (minor tissue loss) distinction can be difficult in neuropathic patients (diabetes).

entries.name: Fontaine Classification of Peripheral Arterial Disease
entries.purpose: Simple clinical staging system for chronic lower extremity ischemia based on symptoms. Used for initial clinical assessment, epidemiological studies, and treatment pathway selection.
entries.formula_human:
Fontaine Classification:

Stage I: Asymptomatic
Stage IIa: Intermittent claudication, walking distance >200 meters
Stage IIb: Intermittent claudication, walking distance ≤200 meters
Stage III: Ischemic rest pain (typically nocturnal, relieved by dependency)
Stage IV: Ischemic ulcers or gangrene of the foot/leg

inputs.label: Clinical stage
inputs.description: Symptom-based classification of chronic PAD severity
inputs.options_text: Stage I (asymptomatic), Stage IIa (mild claudication, >200m), Stage IIb (moderate-severe claudication, ≤200m), Stage III (ischemic rest pain), Stage IV (ulceration/gangrene)

bands.meaning: Asymptomatic PAD detected incidentally. Medical management.
Mild claudication. Exercise therapy, risk factor modification.
Disabling claudication. Exercise therapy, consider revascularization.
Critical limb ischemia (rest pain). Urgent revascularization.
Critical limb ischemia (tissue loss). Urgent revascularization, wound care, amputation risk.

citations.text: Fontaine R, Kim M, Kieny R. Die chirurgische Behandlung der peripheren Durchblutungsstörungen. Helvetica Chirurgica Acta. 1954;21:499-533

entries.limitations: Walking distance is subjective and varies with effort, terrain, and patient motivation. Does not include objective measurements (ABI, toe pressure, TcPO₂). Stage IIa/IIb distinction is imprecise. Does not capture anatomy of disease (aortoiliac vs. femoropopliteal vs. tibial). Less granular than Rutherford classification. Not suitable for clinical trials (Rutherford preferred). Rest pain may be confounded by neuropathy in diabetics. Does not incorporate wound characteristics (WIfI preferred). Does not predict amputation risk. Stage IV is heterogeneous (small toe ulcer vs. extensive gangrene). Cultural and language differences affect interpretation of claudication distance. Bypassing stage III to IV can occur rapidly in some patients.

entries.name: Villalta Score
entries.purpose: Validated clinical scoring system to diagnose and grade severity of post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS) following deep vein thrombosis. Used as the primary outcome measure in PTS clinical trials and for clinical monitoring.
entries.formula_human:
Villalta Score = Sum of 5 symptom scores (0–3 each) + 6 clinical sign scores (0–3 each, except ulcer = 0 or 5)

Maximum score = 5×3 + 5×3 + 5 = 35
(Ulcer: 5 points if present instead of 0–3 range)

inputs.label: Edema
inputs.description: Pitting edema of the affected leg

bands.meaning: No PTS.
Mild PTS.
Moderate PTS.
Severe PTS.
Severe PTS (ulcer automatically qualifies as severe).

citations.text: Villalta S, Bagatella P, Piccioli A, et al. Assessment of validity and reproducibility of a clinical scale for the post-thrombotic syndrome. Haemostasis. 1994;24:158a; Kahn SR, et al. J Thromb Haemost. 2009;7:1992-1997

entries.limitations: Subjective symptom components (pain, heaviness, cramps) are patient-reported and may vary. Inter-observer variability for clinical signs (induration, edema grading). Requires comparison with the contralateral leg (reference leg may also have disease). Edema grading is particularly subjective. Score ≥5 required for PTS diagnosis — single-point threshold can cause misclassification. Does not incorporate imaging (venous reflux or obstruction by duplex). Ulcer scoring (5 points binary) may overweight this sign relative to others. Not validated in patients with bilateral DVT.
