Should be performed at ≥6 months after DVT (earlier assessment may overdiagnose PTS due to residual DVT symptoms). Clinical significance of mild PTS (5–9) debated. Does not differentiate between deep and superficial venous insufficiency contribution to symptoms.
entries.copyright: public domain — published academic scoring system

entries.name: Sinonasal Outcome Test-22
entries.purpose: Validated patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) for chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS). Assesses disease-specific health status and quality of life. Used as primary outcome in CRS clinical trials, surgical outcome studies, and clinical practice tracking.
entries.formula_human:
SNOT-22 total = Sum of all 22 items (each 0–5)
Range: 0–110

Minimum clinically important difference (MCID): ≥8.9 points change

Items:
1. Need to blow nose
2. Sneezing
3. Runny nose
4. Cough
5. Post-nasal discharge
6. Thick nasal discharge
7. Ear fullness
8. Dizziness
9. Ear pain
10. Facial pain/pressure
11. Difficulty falling asleep
12. Wake up at night
13. Lack of good night's sleep
14. Wake up tired
15. Fatigue
16. Reduced productivity
17. Reduced concentration
18. Frustrated/restless/irritable
19. Sad
20. Embarrassed
21. Sense of taste/smell
22. Blockage/congestion of nose

inputs.label: 22 symptom domains
inputs.description: Each of 22 items rated by patient on a 0–5 Likert scale (0 = no problem, 5 = worst possible)

inputs.label: Domain categories
inputs.description: Five domains: Rhinologic symptoms (3 items), Extra-nasal rhinologic symptoms (4 items), Ear/facial symptoms (4 items), Psychological dysfunction (6 items), Sleep dysfunction (5 items)

bands.meaning: Very mild/no significant impact on quality of life.
Mild CRS symptoms. Medical management appropriate.
Moderate CRS. Consider escalation of medical therapy or surgical evaluation.
Severe CRS. Surgical intervention (FESS) often recommended if medical therapy fails.
Very severe CRS. Strong indication for surgical intervention.

citations.text: Hopkins C, Gillett S, Slack R, et al. Psychometric validity of the 22-item Sinonasal Outcome Test. Clin Otolaryngol. 2009;34(5):447-454. PMID: 19793277

entries.limitations: Patient-reported — subjective. May not correlate with objective measures (CT score, endoscopy score). Recall period debated (1 week vs. 2 weeks vs. current symptoms). MCID of 8.9 established for improvement — smaller changes may not be clinically meaningful. Not disease-specific for CRS subtypes (CRSwNP vs. CRSsNP) — may behave differently. Does not capture asthma control, AERD, or allergic rhinitis contribution. Ceiling effect in very severe patients. Floor effect in mild disease. Cultural and language translation variability (validated in >15 languages). Does not replace clinical assessment or CT (Lund-Mackay). SNOT-22 is more time-consuming than SNOT-7. Does not capture patient expectations or satisfaction. Psychological domain may overlap with general depression/anxiety screening.
entries.copyright: public domain — freely available for clinical and research use

entries.name: International Prostate Symptom Score
entries.purpose: Validated patient-reported questionnaire for assessing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Used to quantify symptom severity, guide treatment decisions, and monitor treatment response. Also applicable to women with lower urinary tract symptoms.
entries.formula_human:
IPSS total (symptom score) = sum of 7 symptom items (questions 1–7)
Range: 0–35
QoL score = question 8 (0–6)

Note: QoL is reported separately from symptom score.

inputs.label: Frequency
inputs.description: Need to urinate again </think>�<2 hours after last voiding

inputs.label: Straining
inputs.description: Need to push or strain to begin urination

inputs.label: Nocturia
inputs.description: Number of times getting up to urinate at night

inputs.label: Quality of life (QoL)
inputs.description: If urinary symptoms remained the same for the rest of life, how would you feel?

bands.meaning: Mild symptoms. Watchful waiting, reassurance, lifestyle modifications.
Moderate symptoms. Consider pharmacotherapy (alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, combination, PDE5 inhibitors).
Severe symptoms. Strong consideration for pharmacotherapy or surgical intervention (TURP, HoLEP, UroLift, Rezum, PAE).
Pleased to mostly satisfied. Watchful waiting reasonable.
Mixed to mostly dissatisfied. Treatment recommended.
Unhappy to terrible. Treatment strongly recommended.

citations.text: Barry MJ, Fowler FJ Jr, O'Leary MP, et al. The American Urological Association symptom index for benign prostatic hyperplasia. J Urol. 1992;148(5):1549-1557. PMID: 1279236; Cockett AT, et al. Proceedings of the International Consultation on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH). Paris, 1991

entries.limitations: Self-reported — subjective. Does not correlate with prostate size, post-void residual, or urodynamic obstruction severity. Bother from symptoms varies widely at the same IPSS score. Nocturia may be caused by non-BPH conditions (heart failure, sleep apnea, nocturnal polyuria). Not specific to BPH (may be elevated with UTI, overactive bladder, prostate cancer). QoL item is single-question — limited psychometric depth. Does not capture sexual function (use IIEF, SHIM separately). Cultural and language variation in interpretation. IPSS should not be the sole basis for surgical decisions. Significant placebo response in clinical trials (up to 30% improvement). International versions validated in >30 languages. Females with LUTS can complete IPSS but gender-specific norms not well established. Not sensitive enough to detect small changes in symptoms.

entries.name: Sexual Health Inventory for Men (SHIM) / International Index of Erectile Function – 5
entries.purpose: Brief validated questionnaire for screening and grading severity of erectile dysfunction (ED). Five-item abbreviated version of the 15-item IIEF. Used in clinical practice for initial ED assessment and monitoring treatment response.
entries.formula_human:
SHIM = Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4 + Q5
Range: 1–25

inputs.label: Q1: Confidence in ability to get and keep erection
inputs.description: How do you rate your confidence?

inputs.label: Q2: Erection hardness during sexual stimulation
inputs.description: When stimulated sexually, how often did your erection hard enough for penetration?

inputs.label: Q3: Ability to maintain erection after penetration
inputs.description: During sexual intercourse, how often were you able to maintain your erection?

inputs.label: Q4: Difficulty maintaining erection to completion
inputs.description: During sexual intercourse, how difficult was it to maintain your erection?

inputs.label: Q5: Satisfaction with sexual intercourse
inputs.description: When attempted sexual intercourse, how often was it satisfactory?

bands.meaning: No erectile dysfunction.
Mild ED. Consider lifestyle modifications, PDE5 inhibitor trial.
Mild-to-moderate ED. PDE5 inhibitor therapy, evaluate contributing factors.
Moderate ED. PDE5 inhibitors, consider combination therapy or second-line treatment.
Severe ED. Consider penile Doppler ultrasound, intracavernosal injection, vacuum device, or penile prosthesis.

citations.text: Rosen RC, Cappelleri JC, Smith MD, et al. Development and evaluation of an abridged, 5-item version of the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5) as a diagnostic tool for erectile dysfunction. Int J Impot Res. 1999;11(6):319-326. PMID: 10637462

entries.limitations: Patient-reported — does not include objective measures (RigiScan, penile Doppler, nocturnal penile tumescence). Based on 4-week recall period — may not capture intermittent ED. Does not assess libido, ejaculatory dysfunction, or orgasmic function (use full IIEF-15). May underdiagnose ED in men who are not sexually active. Doesn't capture psychological causes vs. organic causes. Cultural sensitivity varies (some patients reluctant to disclose). Not validated for use in homosexual men or with specific populations. Does not differentiate vasculogenic, neurogenic, hormonal, or psychogenic ED. Cutoff scores may vary by population (age, comorbidities). Not suitable for evaluating Peyronie's disease specifically. No assessment of partner satisfaction.

entries.name: International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire – Urinary Incontinence Short Form
entries.purpose: Validated patient-reported questionnaire for assessing urinary incontinence severity and its impact on quality of life. Used across all types of incontinence (stress, urgency, mixed). Suitable for clinical practice and research.
entries.formula_human:
ICIQ-UI SF score = Q1 (frequency, 0–5) + Q2 (amount, 0–6) + Q3 (impact, 0–10)
Range: 0–21

Additionally: Symptom type identification (Q4a–4d, items not scored but inform diagnosis)

inputs.label: Frequency of leakage
inputs.description: How often do you leak urine?
inputs.options_text: 0 (never), 1 (about once a week or less), 2 (2–3 times a week), 3 (about once a day), 4 (several times a day), 5 (all the time)

inputs.label: Amount of leakage
inputs.description: How much urine do you usually leak?

inputs.label: Overall impact
inputs.description: How much does leaking urine interfere with your everyday life?

bands.meaning: No incontinence.
Slight incontinence. Conservative management (pelvic floor exercises, lifestyle changes).
Moderate incontinence. Consider supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy, pharmacotherapy, or referral.
Severe incontinence. Specialist referral, consider surgical intervention.
Very severe incontinence. Urgent specialist evaluation. Consider invasive treatment.

citations.text: Avery K, Donovan J, Peters TJ, et al. ICIQ: a brief and robust measure for evaluating the symptoms and impact of urinary incontinence. Neurourol Urodyn. 2004;23(4):322-330. PMID: 15227639

entries.limitations: Patient-reported — does not include objective measures (pad test, urodynamics). Does not distinguish between stress, urgency, and mixed incontinence (items are for symptom type, not scoring). Doesn't capture frequency-volume chart data. Q3 (impact) is subjective and may be influenced by coping strategies. Not validated for neurogenic bladder populations. Not suitable for assessing post-surgical outcomes without baseline comparison. May not be sensitive to small treatment changes. Does not assess nocturia specifically. No gender-specific normative data.
entries.copyright: public domain — freely available at iciq.net

entries.name: Kidney Donor Profile Index
entries.purpose: Percentile score summarizing deceased donor kidney quality based on 10 donor factors. Combines donor age, height, weight, ethnicity, hypertension history, diabetes history, cause of death, serum creatinine, HCV status, and DCD status. Higher KDPI = lower expected graft survival.
entries.formula_human:
KDPI = percentile ranking of donor Expected Post-Transplant Survival (EPTS) among all deceased donors in the prior year

KDPI = combined donor quality score (0–100%)

Lower KDPI = better quality kidney (better expected graft survival)
Higher KDPI = lower quality kidney (shorter expected graft survival)

Note: KDPI 0% is theoretically the best possible donor kidney; 100% is the worst.

KDPI replaces the older Donor Risk Index (DRI).

inputs.label: Donor age
inputs.description: Age of deceased donor in years

bands.meaning: High-quality kidneys. Excellent expected graft survival (>12 years). Standard allocation.
Average-quality kidneys. Acceptable for most recipients.

Lower-quality kidneys. Shorter expected graft survival. Consider for older recipients, those with long dialysis time, or those willing to accept higher KDPI. Kidneys with KDPI >85% may be declined by some centers.

citations.text: Rao PS, Schaubel DE, Guidinger MK, et al. A comprehensive risk quantification score for deceased donor kidneys: the Kidney Donor Risk Index. Transplantation. 2009;88(2):231-236. PMID: 19623010; OPTN/SRTR 2012 Annual Data Report

entries.limitations: Does not capture biopsy findings (chronicity score, glomerulosclerosis). Doesn't capture cold ischemia time (CIT) — major factor in graft survival. Doesn't capture donor-specific antibodies (DSA) status. Doesn't capture warm ischemia time for DCD. KDPI >85% does not mean kidney is unsuitable — allocation policy debates ongoing. Doesn't incorporate machine perfusion parameters. Doesn't capture donor BMI-specific metabolic risk. Based on US donor population — may not be generalizable internationally. Percentile shifts annually based on donor pool. Doesn't predict individual kidney survival with certainty — population-level estimate. Some centers use KDPI >85% as 'extended criteria' threshold, but this is center-dependent. Doesn't account for recipient factors (use EPTS for recipient quality matching). Living donor kidneys do not have KDPI — use Living Donor Risk Index separately.
entries.copyright: OPTN/UNOS — free for clinical use (calculated by SRTR/OPTN)

entries.name: Banff Classification of Renal Allograft Pathology
entries.purpose: International standardized classification system for renal allograft biopsies. Provides diagnostic categories for T-cell mediated rejection (TCMR), antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR), and other transplant pathologies. Updated every 2 years at Banff conferences.
entries.formula_human:
Banff 2019 Diagnostic Categories:

1. Normal
2. Antibody-mediated changes (ABMR):
   - Active ABMR: g>0 OR ptc>0 + C4d>0 OR molecular markers + DSA
   - Chronic active ABMR: chronic glomerulopathy + active ABMR features
   - Chronic (inactive) ABMR: chronic changes + C4d + no activity
3. T-cell mediated rejection (TCMR):
   - Borderline changes: i≥1 and/or t≥1 (i0t0 allowed if v>0)
   - Acute TCMR:
     IA: i≥2, t≥2 (significant i + moderate t)
     IB: i≥2, t≥3 (significant i + severe t)
     IIA: v1 (mild arteritis)
     IIB: v2 (moderate arteritis)
     III: v3 (severe transmural arteritis)
   - Chronic active TCMR: TCMR features + chronic allograft arteriopathy
4. IFTA (interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy) without specific etiology:
   Grade I (ci1-2 + ct1-2), Grade II (ci2-3 + ct2), Grade III (ci3 + ct3)
5. Other: Calcineurin inhibitor toxicity, BK nephropathy, recurrent disease, etc.

inputs.label: i (interstitial inflammation)
inputs.description: Percentage of cortex with inflammation (excluding areas of sclerosis/atrophy)

inputs.label: t (tubulitis)
inputs.description: Mononuclear cells per tubular cross-section in non-atrophic tubules
inputs.options_text: t0 (none), t1 (1–4 cells/tubule), t2 (5–10 cells/tubule), t3 (>10 cells/tubule)

inputs.label: v (intimal arteritis)
inputs.options_text: v0 (none), v1 (mild — </think>�<25% of circumference), v2 (moderate — ≥25% of circumference), v3 (transmural arteritis/fibrinoid necrosis)

inputs.label: g (glomerulitis)
inputs.options_text: g0 (</think>�<10% glomeruli), g1 (mild increase), g2 (moderate increase), g3 (severe increase)

inputs.label: ptc (peritubular capillaritis)
inputs.options_text: ptc0 (none), ptc1 (1–5 cells/ptc cross-section), ptc2 (6–10), ptc3 (>10)

inputs.label: C4d staining
inputs.description: Complement C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries by immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry

inputs.label: ci (interstitial fibrosis)
inputs.description: Percentage of cortex with fibrosis (IFTA — interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy)

inputs.label: ct (tubular atrophy)
inputs.description: Percentage of tubules that are atrophic

inputs.label: cv (vascular fibrous intimal thickening)
inputs.options_text: cv0 (none), cv1 (mild — </think>�<25% lumen narrowing), cv2 (moderate — 26–50%), cv3 (severe — >50%)

inputs.label: IFTA score
inputs.description: Combined interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy

bands.meaning: Mild interstitial inflammation ± tubulitis. Consider subclinical rejection vs. other causes. May require treatment or monitoring.
Tubulo-interstitial rejection without vasculitis. Treat with pulse steroids.
Severe tubulo-interstitial rejection. Treat with pulse steroids, consider anti-thymocyte globulin.
Arteritis present. Aggressive immunosuppression. Poorer prognosis than IA/IB.
Transmural arteritis/fibrinoid necrosis. Very poor prognosis. Aggressive treatment but graft loss common.
Antibody-mediated rejection. Treat with plasmapheresis, IVIG, rituximab, bortezomib, eculizumab, or complement inhibitors.
Chronic allograft injury. Irreversible. Optimize remaining nephrons, adjust immunosuppression, manage risk factors.

citations.text: Loupy A, Haas M, Roufosse C, et al. The Banff 2019 Kidney Meeting Report. Am J Transplant. 2020;20(3):587-603. PMID: 31943670; Racusen LC, et al. Kidney Int. 1999;55:713-723

entries.limitations: Requires experienced transplant pathologist for accurate scoring. Inter-observer variability exists (especially for i, t, g, ptc scores). C4d-negative ABMR now recognized — C4d alone insufficient. Molecular markers (gene expression, dd-cfDNA) increasingly important but not universally available. Biopsy sampling error (15-gauge needle may miss focal lesions). Category boundaries are somewhat arbitrary. Treatment algorithms based on Banff categories vary by center. Borderline changes management is debated. Chronic changes (IFTA) are irreversible — limited treatment options. Classification evolves with each Banff conference — not static. Some categories overlap. Does not capture recurrence of original disease. Does not fully address combined rejection and infection (e.g., BK + rejection). TCMR vs. ABMR distinction may be artificial (overlap exists).
entries.copyright: public domain — international consensus, free for clinical use

entries.name: Rapid Emergency Medicine Score
entries.purpose: Quick bedside scoring system for predicting in-hospital mortality in emergency department patients. Uses 6 readily available physiologic variables. Derived from APACHE II and designed for rapid application in the ED setting.
entries.formula_human:
REMS = Age points + HR points + SBP points + RR points + GCS points + SpO₂ points
Range: 0–38

inputs.label: SpO₂ (or PaO₂ if available)
inputs.options_text: 0 (SpO₂ ≥90% or PaO₂ ≥70), 2 (SpO₂ 86–89% or PaO₂ 60–69), 4 (SpO₂ 75–85% or PaO₂ 55–59), 7 (SpO₂ </think>�<75% or PaO₂ </think>�<55)

bands.meaning: Very low mortality risk (~1–2%)
Low mortality risk (~5–10%)
Moderate mortality risk (~15–30%)
High mortality risk (~40–60%)
Very high mortality risk (~>70%)

citations.text: Olsson T, Lind L. Comparison of the Rapid Emergency Medicine Score and APACHE II in nonsurgical emergency patients. Acad Emerg Med. 2003;10(10):1040-1048. PMID: 14525733

entries.limitations: Designed for general ED population — may not perform well in specific subgroups (trauma, pediatrics, obstetric). Does not incorporate comorbidities or diagnosis. Single-time measurement — doesn't capture trajectory. Laboratory values not included (unlike APACHE II). Performance varies by ED population (university vs. community). Does not predict ICU admission directly — only mortality. Not validated in prehospital setting (despite name EMS). May underestimate risk in patients with chronic vital sign abnormalities. Not suitable for pediatric patients.
entries.copyright: public domain — published academic scoring system

entries.name: Los Angeles Motor Scale
entries.category: prehospital large vessel occlusion stroke screening
entries.purpose: Prehospital screening tool to identify patients with suspected large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke for direct transport to comprehensive stroke centers (bypassing primary stroke centers). Derived from the Los Angeles Prehospital Stroke Screen (LAPSS).
entries.formula_human:
LAMS = Facial droop + Arm drift + Grip strength
Range: 0–6

inputs.label: Arm drift
inputs.description: Arm weakness assessment (10 seconds, arms outstretched)

inputs.label: Grip strength
inputs.options_text: 0 (normal grip), 1 (weak grip, not able to maintain grip against examiner), 2 (no grip)

bands.meaning: Low probability of LVO. Transport to nearest stroke-capable facility (primary stroke center acceptable).
High probability of LVO. Direct transport to comprehensive stroke center (capable of thrombectomy). Bypass primary stroke center if time allows.

citations.text: Llanes JN, Kidwell CS, Starkman S, et al. The Los Angeles Motor Scale (LAMS): a new measure to characterize stroke severity in the field. Prehosp Emerg Care. 2004;8(1):46-50. PMID: 14691789

entries.limitations: Designed for anterior circulation LVO — does not capture posterior circulation strokes. Sensitivity for LVO detection varies (66–93% across studies). May miss distal MCA occlusions or subtle presentations. Does not assess for aphasia, neglect, or visual field deficits. Binary cutoff (≥4) may miss some LVO patients. Training required for prehospital personnel. Not validated in all EMS settings. False-positive LAMS ≥4 may lead to unnecessary bypass of primary stroke center. Performance depends on time from symptom onset. Not a substitute for comprehensive neurological assessment. Does not replace CT angiography for LVO confirmation.

entries.name: Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale
entries.purpose: Rapid bedside screening tool for prehospital and emergency stroke detection. Assesses three physical findings to identify potential stroke patients for rapid transport to stroke-capable facilities. Derived from the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS).
entries.formula_human:
CPSS = Number of abnormal findings (0–3)
Each abnormal finding = 1 point

inputs.label: Facial droop
inputs.description: Have patient smile or show teeth. Look for asymmetry.
inputs.options_text: Normal (both sides move equally), Abnormal (one side does not move as well or droops)

inputs.label: Arm drift
inputs.description: Have patient close eyes and hold both arms out for 10 seconds. Look for one arm drifting down.
inputs.options_text: Normal (both arms move equally or not at all), Abnormal (one arm drifts down or does not move)

inputs.label: Speech
inputs.description: Have patient repeat 'You can't teach an old dog new tricks.' Assess for slurred or inappropriate speech.
inputs.options_text: Normal (clear speech with correct words), Abnormal (slurred speech, wrong words, or unable to speak)

bands.meaning: No stroke signs identified. Low probability of stroke. Continue assessment.
Possible stroke. 72% probability of stroke diagnosis. Activate stroke protocol and transport to stroke center.
Probable stroke. >85% probability. Rapid transport to comprehensive stroke center.
Highly probable stroke. >95% probability. Emergency transport, consider large vessel occlusion (LVO) screening.

citations.text: Kothari RU, Pancioli A, Liu T, et al. Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale: reproducibility and validity. Ann Emerg Med. 1999;33(4):373-378. PMID: 10092713

entries.limitations: Screening tool only — does not quantify stroke severity or distinguish stroke subtypes. Does not identify large vessel occlusion (LVO) — use RACE, LAMS, FAST-ED, or NIHSS for LVO detection. Sensitivity varies by stroke location (posterior stroke often missed). Single arm drift may miss subtle findings (leg weakness, sensory loss, visual field defect). Does not assess for posterior circulation symptoms (vertigo, diplopia, ataxia). Prehospital use requires brief training. Limited to 3 binary findings — coarser than NIHSS. Negative CPSS does not rule out stroke (sensitivity ~60-70%). Doesn't capture time of symptom onset (critical for tPA eligibility). Not validated for TIA diagnosis. False negatives in patients with posterior circulation strokes, small lacunar strokes, or primarily sensory deficits. Does not replace comprehensive neurological assessment.

entries.name: Confusion Assessment Method
entries.purpose: Standardized bedside tool for detecting delirium in hospitalized patients. Most widely used delirium screening instrument internationally. Uses 4 criteria derived from DSM diagnostic criteria for delirium. Also has ICU version (CAM-ICU) for intubated/non-verbal patients.
entries.formula_human:
CAM positive (delirium present) = Feature 1 AND Feature 2 AND (Feature 3 OR Feature 4)

Acute onset/fluctuating course (1) + Inattention (2) + Disorganized thinking (3) OR Altered consciousness (4) = Delirium

CAM-ICU: Modified for ICU (uses sedation assessment first, then attention test, then organized thinking, then acute change)

inputs.label: Feature 1: Acute onset and fluctuating course
Feature 4: Altered level of consciousness
inputs.description: Is the patient's level of consciousness anything other than alert (vigilant, lethargic, stupor, coma, hypervigilant)?
inputs.options_text: Alert (normal) vs. Altered (vigilant, lethargic, stupor, coma)

bands.meaning: Delirium present. Identify and treat underlying cause(s) (infection, medications, metabolic derangement, pain, constipation, urinary retention, alcohol withdrawal, sleep deprivation). Ensure patient safety. Consider geriatric/psychiatry consult.
Delirium not detected. Continue routine monitoring. Reassess regularly (especially if risk factors present).

citations.text: Inouye SK, van Dyck CH, Alessi CA, et al. Clarifying confusion: the Confusion Assessment Method. A new method for detection of delirium. Ann Intern Med. 1990;113(12):941-948. PMID: 2240918

entries.limitations: Requires trained assessor for reliable application. Feature 1 (acute onset/fluctuating course) may be difficult to assess if baseline mental status unknown. Fluctuation requires serial assessments — single-time application may miss delirium. Subtypes (hyperactive, hypoactive, mixed) not distinguished — hypoactive delirium may be missed. Sensitivity varies by training level of assessor (47–94%). CAM-ICU requires RASS ≥-3 (deeply sedated patients cannot be assessed). Does not distinguish delirium from dementia (dementia is a risk factor). Requires at least 5 minutes to perform — may not be feasible in busy settings. Not validated in children (use pCAM-ICU or CAPD). Does not capture severity (use CAM-S for severity scoring). False negatives possible with hypoactive delirium. Not a substitute for comprehensive delirium evaluation. Does not identify the cause of delirium.
entries.copyright: Dr. Sharon Inouye — free for clinical use (copyright retained)

entries.name: Hendrich II Fall Risk Model
entries.purpose: Validated fall risk assessment tool for hospitalized adults. Uses eight risk factors to identify patients at risk for falls. Designed to be quick to administer and evidence-based. Alternative to Morse Fall Scale.
entries.formula_human:
Hendrich II = Confusion + Depression + Altered elimination + Dizziness + Gender + Antiepileptic/Benzodiazepine + TUG score + Weakness/fatigue
Range: 0–23

inputs.label: Short Timed Up and Go (TUG) test performance
inputs.description: Ability to rise from chair, walk 3 meters, turn, walk back, and sit down. Score based on time and independence.
inputs.options_text: 0 (able to rise in single movement, no imbalance), 1 (pushes up, successful in one attempt), 2 (multiple attempts but able), 3–4 (unable without assistance / not attempted)

bands.meaning: Standard fall precautions. Routine care.
Implement fall prevention interventions. Targeted care plan based on specific risk factors identified.

citations.text: Hendrich AL, Bender PS, Nyhuis A. Validation of the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model: a large concurrent case/control study of hospitalized patients. Appl Nurs Res. 2003;16(1):9-21. PMID: 12624857

entries.limitations: TUG test may not be feasible for all patients (bedridden, very weak, confused). Assessment takes longer than Morse Fall Scale. Not validated in all hospital populations (ICU, psychiatric, pediatric). Confusion assessment is subjective. Depression screening is limited to documented diagnosis or medication use. Antiepileptic/benzodiazepine component gets very high weight (7 points) — may dominate the score. Not validated in long-term care settings. Different cutoff values used by different institutions. 'Altered elimination' is broad — includes multiple conditions. Does not capture environmental fall risks. Single-time assessment — should be reassessed regularly. Less widely used than Morse Fall Scale (limited external validation). Not suitable for ED triage.

entries.name: Braden Scale for Predicting Pressure Sore Risk
entries.purpose: Standardized nursing assessment tool for predicting pressure injury risk in hospitalized and long-term care patients. Guides preventive interventions (turning schedule, pressure redistribution surfaces, nutrition support). Most widely used pressure injury risk assessment tool internationally.
entries.formula_human:
Braden Score = Sensory perception + Moisture + Activity + Mobility + Nutrition + Friction and shear
Range: 6–23

inputs.label: Sensory perception
inputs.description: Ability to respond meaningfully to pressure-related discomfort

inputs.label: Moisture
inputs.description: Degree to which skin is exposed to moisture

inputs.label: Mobility
inputs.description: Ability to change and control body position

inputs.label: Friction and shear
inputs.description: Degree of friction and shear on skin
inputs.options_text: 1 (problem — requires moderate to maximum assistance, slides frequently), 2 (potential problem — moves feebly, requires some assistance), 3 (no apparent problem — moves in bed independently)

bands.meaning: No risk / Very mild risk. Standard prevention protocols. Reassess on admission and with condition change.
Mild risk. Pressure redistribution surface, turning schedule, nutrition optimization, skin assessment every shift.
Moderate risk. Specialty pressure-redistributing surface (alternating pressure mattress), 2-hourly repositioning, nutrition consult.
High risk. Advanced pressure-redistributing surface (low-air-loss or alternating pressure mattress), 2-hourly repositioning, heel elevation, nutrition support, moisture management.
Very high risk. Critical care level prevention (air-fluidized bed or equivalent), frequent repositioning, comprehensive skin care, nutrition optimization, multidisciplinary approach.

citations.text: Bergstrom N, Demuth PJ, Braden BJ. A clinical trial of the Braden Scale for Predicting Pressure Sore Risk. Nurs Clin North Am. 1987;22(2):417-428. PMID: 3299494; Braden BJ, Bergstrom N. Nurs Res. 1987;36:205-210

entries.limitations: Assessing 'sensory perception' and 'moisture' can be subjective. Not validated for all patient populations (neonates, pediatrics). Sensitivity and specificity vary by cutoff score and population. Does not capture all risk factors (skin condition, medication, perfusion status). Reassessment frequency varies by institutional protocol (minimum weekly and with condition change). Not suitable for predicting medical device-related pressure injuries. Overprediction of risk in low-risk populations (high false-positive rate). Underprediction in some high-risk groups (darkly pigmented skin — skin assessment challenges). Nutrition component is subjective (nurses may not accurately assess intake). Friction/shear is the hardest component to score reliably. Must be combined with clinical judgment — score alone is insufficient for prevention planning.

entries.name: Mallampati Classification
entries.purpose: Preoperative airway assessment tool to predict difficult laryngoscopy and intubation. Visual assessment of the oropharyngeal structures visible with maximal mouth opening and tongue protrusion. Part of comprehensive airway assessment (should not be used in isolation).
entries.formula_human:
Mallampati Classification (Samsoon & Young modification):

Class I: Soft palate, uvula, fauces, anterior and posterior pillars visible
Class II: Soft palate, uvula, fauces visible
Class III: Soft palate, base of uvula visible
Class IV: Hard palate only visible (soft palate not visible)

Note: Patient should be seated upright, mouth fully open, tongue maximally protruded. No phonation during assessment.

inputs.label: Oropharyngeal view
inputs.description: Structures visible with patient seated, mouth maximally open, tongue protruding maximally (without phonation)

bands.meaning: Easy intubation expected. Full visualization of structures. Low probability of difficult intubation (~1%).
Likely easy intubation. Most structures visible. Low probability (~5%).
Potentially difficult intubation. Only soft palate and base of uvula visible. Moderate probability (~20%).
Difficult intubation likely. Only hard palate visible. High probability (~35–50%). Prepare for difficult airway.

citations.text: Mallampati SR, Gatt SP, Gugino LD, et al. A clinical sign to predict difficult tracheal intubation: a prospective study. Can Anaesth Soc J. 1985;32(4):429-434. PMID: 4027773; Samsoon GLT, Young JRB. Anaesthesia. 1987;42:487-490

entries.limitations: Subjective assessment — inter-rater variability. Single predictor of difficult intubation — must be combined with other factors (thyromental distance, neck mobility, mouth opening, upper lip bite test, body habitus). Poor positive predictive value (~50% of Mallampati IV are still intubatable). Patient cooperation required (pain, confusion, or altered consciousness limit assessment). Position affects grading (sniffing position vs. sitting). Phonation during assessment elevates the palate — may artificially improve grade. Obesity, large tongue, or macroglossia may limit view. Does not predict difficult mask ventilation (separate assessment needed). Not validated in pediatric populations (modified assessment needed). Mallampati I–II does not guarantee easy intubation. Difficult intubation is multifactorial — no single test is sufficient. High sensitivity but low specificity for difficult intubation prediction. No single airway assessment test has both high sensitivity and specificity.

entries.name: Apfel Simplified Risk Score for Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
entries.category: postoperative nausea and vomiting risk prediction
entries.purpose: Simplified scoring system for predicting the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in adult surgical patients. Guides antiemetic prophylaxis decisions. Designed for ease of use in preoperative assessment.
entries.formula_human:
Apfel Score = Female + Non-smoker + History of motion sickness/PONV + Postoperative opioid use
Range: 0–4

inputs.label: Non-smoking status
inputs.description: Patient is a non-smoker (or has not smoked for ≥2 weeks preoperatively)

inputs.label: History of motion sickness or PONV

bands.meaning: ~10% PONV risk. Low risk. Routine care. Prophylaxis not typically needed.
~20% PONV risk. Low-moderate risk. Consider single antiemetic prophylaxis.
~40% PONV risk. Moderate risk. Recommend dual antiemetic prophylaxis.
~60% PONV risk. High risk. Multimodal antiemetic strategy (≥2 antiemetics, consider TIVA, regional anesthesia).

~80% PONV risk. Very high risk. Aggressive multimodal prophylaxis (≥3 antiemetics, TIVA, avoid nitrous oxide/volatile agents, regional if possible, dexamethasone + ondansetron + droperidol ± scopolamine).

citations.text: Apfel CC, Läärä E, Koivuranta M, et al. A simplified risk score for predicting postoperative nausea and vomiting: conclusions from cross-validations between two centers. Anesthesiology. 1999;91(3):693-700. PMID: 10485781

entries.limitations: Based on 4 risk factors only — does not capture all PONV risk (type/duration of surgery, history of migraine, anxiety, ASA status, age). Applies to adults only (not pediatric). Opioid use is predicted, not confirmed preoperatively. Smoker status: patients must have abstained for ≥2 weeks to qualify as 'non-smoker.' Does not distinguish between nausea and vomiting. Does not guide specific antiemetic choice (only triggers prophylaxis threshold). Threshold for 'high risk' may vary by institutional practice. Not validated for specific surgical types (laparoscopy vs. open vs. neurosurgery). May overestimate risk in some populations (outpatient surgery). Does not capture severity of PONV. Risk estimates are approximate — individual risk varies. Does not incorporate intraoperative factors (volatile agents, fluid management). PONV-25 may be more discriminating but is less simple.

entries.name: American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification
entries.purpose: Standardized classification of a patient's preoperative physical health status. Used globally for preoperative assessment, communication among anesthesia providers, risk stratification, and resource allocation. Not intended as a surgical risk score — assesses patient health, not surgical complexity.
entries.formula_human:
ASA Physical Status:

ASA I: A normal healthy patient (no organic, physiologic, or psychiatric disturbance)
ASA II: A patient with mild systemic disease (e.g., well-controlled HTN, DM, obesity with BMI 30–40, social drinking, mild lung disease, pregnancy)
ASA III: A patient with severe systemic disease (e.g., poorly controlled HTN or DM, COPD, morbid obesity BMI ≥40, active hepatitis, alcohol dependence/abuse, implanted pacemaker, moderate reduction in ejection fraction, ESRD with dialysis, prior MI/CVA/TIA, CAD/stents)
ASA IV: A patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (e.g., recent MI/CVA, ongoing cardiac ischemia, severe valve dysfunction, sepsis, DIC, ARDS, ESRD not regularly dialyzed)
ASA V: A moribund patient who is not expected to survive without the operation (e.g., ruptured AAA, massive trauma, intracranial bleed with mass effect, cardiac tamponade, bowel infarction)
ASA VI: A declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes

E modifier: Emergency — append 'E' to any class (e.g., ASA IIIE)

inputs.label: ASA Physical Status
inputs.description: Anesthesiologist's assessment of the patient's overall health
inputs.options_text: ASA I through ASA VI (with E modifier for emergency)

bands.meaning: Healthy. Low anesthetic risk. Mortality very low (~0.01%).
Mild systemic disease. Low risk. Mortality ~0.02–0.05%.
Severe systemic disease. Moderate risk. Mortality ~0.1–0.5%.
Severe systemic disease, constant threat to life. High risk. Mortality ~1–5%.
Moribund. Very high risk. Mortality ~10–50%.
Brain-dead organ donor.
Emergency case. Any emergency has higher risk than elective equivalent.

citations.text: Saklad M. Grading of patients for surgical procedures. Anesthesiology. 1941;2:281-284; ASA Physical Status Classification System. 2014 (updated examples); Hurwitz EE, et al. Anesth Analg. 2017;124:2001-2006

entries.limitations: Subjective classification — inter-rater agreement is moderate (~60–70%). Significant variability between anesthesiologists for ASA II vs. III and III vs. IV. Does not account for surgical complexity. Does not incorporate age, body habitus (unless extreme), or functional capacity. Not designed as a surgical risk score (though correlated with outcomes). Emergency modifier (E) adds risk but not quantified. Some institutions use half-grades (e.g., ASA II/III) — non-standardized. Should be used in conjunction with surgical risk calculators (ACS NSQIP, RCRI). Does not capture specific organ system dysfunction. ASA I patients can still have difficult airway or other anesthesia-specific risks. Updated examples in 2014 improved standardization but inter-rater variability persists. Not validated for office-based or ambulatory surgery populations specifically. ASA VI designation has limited clinical use (organ procurement cases only).

entries.name: World Allergy Organization Diagnostic Criteria for Anaphylaxis
entries.purpose: International diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis, a severe, potentially life-threatening systemic allergic reaction. Provides clinical decision rules for rapid diagnosis and treatment initiation. Used by WAO, NIAID/FAAN, and international guidelines.
entries.formula_human:
Anaphylaxis is highly likely when ANY ONE of the following 3 criteria is met:

Criterion 1: Acute onset (minutes to hours) of skin/mucosal symptoms (urticaria, flushing, pruritus, angioedema) AND at least one of:
  a) Respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia)
  b) Cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, end-organ dysfunction)

Criterion 2: Rapid onset (minutes to hours) of ≥2 of the following after exposure to a LIKELY allergen:
  a) Skin/mucosal involvement
  b) Respiratory compromise
  c) Cardiovascular compromise
  d) Persistent GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, crampy abdominal pain, diarrhea)

Criterion 3: Reduced blood pressure (minutes to hours) after exposure to a KNOWN allergen:
  Adult: SBP </think>�<90 mmHg or >30% decrease from baseline
  Child (1–12 years): Low SBP for age or >30% decrease in SBP
  Infant (</think>�<1 year): Low SBP for age or >30% decrease in SBP

inputs.label: Criterion 2: Rapid onset of ≥2 organ systems
inputs.description: After exposure to a LIKELY allergen: skin/mucosal + respiratory + cardiovascular + GI (nausea, vomiting, crampy abdominal pain, diarrhea)

inputs.label: Criterion 3: Hypotension after exposure to KNOWN allergen

bands.meaning: Anaphylaxis diagnosed. IMMEDIATE TREATMENT: Epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM (adults) or 0.01 mg/kg IM (children, max 0.3 mg) into anterolateral thigh. Call for help. Position supine with legs elevated. Supplemental oxygen. IV fluids (1–2L NS bolus). Second-line: H1-antihistamine, H2-antihistamine, bronchodilator, corticosteroid. Monitor for biphasic reaction (4–12 hours).

bands.range: Criteria not met but clinical concern
bands.meaning: Anaphylaxis not confirmed. Observe closely. May be early anaphylaxis or evolving reaction. Have epinephrine ready.

citations.text: Sampson HA, Muñoz-Furlong A, Campbell RL, et al. Second symposium on the definition and management of anaphylaxis: summary report. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2006;117(2):391-397. PMID: 16461139; Cardona V, et al. World Allergy Organ J. 2020;13(1):100006 (WAO criteria update)

entries.limitations: Skin symptoms may be absent in up to 20% of anaphylaxis episodes (especially perioperative, during anesthesia, or in patients on immunosuppressants). Hypotension may be the only initial sign. Biphasic anaphylaxis (second wave 4–12 hours after initial reaction) is not predicted by initial severity. Criteria apply to IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated anaphylaxis but may miss some anaphylactoid reactions. Epinephrine is underused — delay in administration increases mortality. IM route is standard — IV epinephrine only for refractory shock with cardiac monitoring. Beta-blocker use may mask symptoms and reduce epinephrine effectiveness. Criteria are clinical — laboratory confirmation (tryptase) is supportive but not diagnostic in real-time. Do not use for research definition without laboratory confirmation. Anaphylaxis in infants may be difficult to recognize (vague symptoms). Exercise-induced and idiopathic anaphylaxis may have atypical presentations. Criteria may be difficult to apply in prehospital or resource-limited settings. Not all patients who meet criteria will have classic presentation. Mast cell tryptase (baseline + 1–2 hours + 24 hours) should be measured to confirm but does not rule out.

entries.name: Global Initiative for Asthma Stepwise Approach
entries.purpose: International evidence-based framework for asthma diagnosis, assessment, and management. Provides stepwise treatment approach based on symptom control and future risk. Updated annually by GINA Science Committee.
entries.formula_human:
GINA Asthma Control Assessment:

WELL-CONTROLLED: None of the following (daytime symptoms ≤2x/week, no night waking, reliever use ≤2x/week, no activity limitation)

PARTLY CONTROLLED: 1–2 of the above present

UNCONTROLLED: 3–4 of the above present

GINA Treatment Steps (2023-2024):
Step 1: As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (preferred) or as-needed SABA + low-dose ICS
Step 2: Daily low-dose ICS + as-needed SABA (or low-dose ICS-formoterol maintenance + as-needed)
Step 3: Low-dose ICS-LABA maintenance + as-needed (preferred: budesonide-formoterol MART)
Step 4: Medium-dose ICS-LABA + as-needed (preferred: medium-dose budesonide-formoterol MART)
Step 5: High-dose ICS-LABA + add-on (anti-IgE, anti-IL5/5R, anti-IL4R, anti-TSLP, low-dose azithromycin, low-dose OCS as last resort) + referral to severe asthma specialist

inputs.label: Symptom control
inputs.description: Assessed by GINA symptom control questions (past 4 weeks)

inputs.label: Exacerbations in past year
inputs.description: Number of exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids in the past 12 months

bands.meaning: Mild asthma. As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol preferred. SABA-only no longer recommended (increased exacerbation risk).
Mild persistent asthma. Daily low-dose ICS. Most effective controller for mild asthma.
Moderate asthma. Low-dose ICS-LABA. MART (maintenance and reliever therapy) preferred.
Moderate-to-severe asthma. Medium-dose ICS-LABA. Check adherence, inhaler technique, and comorbidities before escalating.
Severe asthma. Referral to specialist. Consider biologics (type 2 inflammation) or bronchial thermoplasty. Low-dose OCS as last resort.

citations.text: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA). Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention. 2023 Report. Available from: www.ginasthma.org

entries.limitations: Step assignments are approximate — some patients fall between steps. MART approach is preferred by GINA but not universally available (budesonide-formoterol specific). 'As-needed ICS-formoterol' approach replaces SABA-only in mild asthma — significant practice change. Biologic selection requires specific biomarkers (blood eosinophils, FeNO, IgE) — not available in all settings. Adherence and inhaler technique are critical but frequently suboptimal. Asthma-COPD overlap not fully addressed. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction management is briefly covered. Not validated for children </think>�<6 years (different stepping). Severe asthma definition varies (uncontrolled on step 4-5 vs. requires OCS). Type 2 vs. non-type 2 asthma distinction not always clear. Pregnancy-related modifications needed (most ICS safe, but specific recommendations). Cost of biologics limits access. Occupational asthma requires specific management (removal from exposure) not covered in stepping.
